content:
## A Fictional 2025 Interview with Steve Jobs on the Future of AI

*The following is an imagined interview. Steve Jobs died in 2011; these answers are fictional and based loosely on his publicly known product philosophy—not authentic quotations.*

**Interviewer:** Steve, everyone in technology is talking about artificial intelligence. Is AI the next great computing revolution?

**Steve Jobs:** AI isn’t the revolution by itself. The revolution happens when it disappears into products people love.

Nobody bought a Macintosh because they wanted a graphical user interface. They wanted to write, design, learn, and create without fighting the computer. AI will matter when we stop advertising how many parameters a model has and start asking: *What can a person do today that felt impossible yesterday?*

---

**Interviewer:** What’s wrong with today’s AI products?

**Jobs:** Most of them feel like demonstrations.

They give you a blank box and say, “Ask me anything.” That’s impressive for five minutes, but it puts all the responsibility on the user. Great products don’t merely expose technology; they make choices. They understand the moment you’re in, remove unnecessary steps, and give you confidence.

The winning AI product won’t feel like a chatbot bolted onto every application. It will feel like the application finally understands why you opened it.

---

**Interviewer:** Would you build an AI device?

**Jobs:** I wouldn’t begin with a device. I’d begin with the experience.

What is missing from people’s lives? Maybe it’s a computer that understands your intentions without demanding constant attention. Maybe it helps you organize your work, communicate clearly, or create something beautiful. Then you ask what combination of hardware, software, and services makes that possible.

Starting with “Let’s make an AI gadget” is how you end up with a solution looking for a problem.

---

**Interviewer:** Does AI make the smartphone obsolete?

**Jobs:** People love declaring things dead. Usually, they’re wrong.

The smartphone won’t disappear because somebody made a clever assistant. But its role could change. Today, you navigate through apps to reach capabilities. AI could invert that relationship: you express what you want, and the system assembles the right capabilities for you.

But screens are useful. Touch is useful. Cameras are useful. Voice is useful sometimes—and terrible in a crowded room. The future isn’t one interface replacing all the others. It’s the right interface appearing at the right moment.

---

**Interviewer:** What would an Apple-like AI assistant look like?

**Jobs:** It would know enough to be helpful and reveal little enough to be trustworthy.

It would operate across your devices without making you understand the plumbing. It would help draft a message but preserve your voice. It would summarize your day without inventing facts. It would take action only when it understood the consequences—and when it wasn’t sure, it would ask.

Most importantly, it would have taste. Intelligence without taste gives you an infinite number of mediocre choices.

---

**Interviewer:** AI systems sometimes provide false information. Is that just an engineering problem?

**Jobs:** It’s a product integrity problem.

If a calculator is wrong five percent of the time, you don’t call it magical. You call it broken. AI companies sometimes want credit for what the system can do without accepting responsibility for what it gets wrong.

A trustworthy product needs to understand uncertainty. It should distinguish between knowing, inferring, and guessing. Saying “I don’t know” can be a feature.

---

**Interviewer:** What about privacy?

**Jobs:** Privacy is not a settings page with forty switches. Privacy means the product was designed so it doesn’t need to collect everything in the first place.

AI creates an enormous temptation to vacuum up people’s messages, photographs, voices, locations, and habits. Companies will say the data makes the system better. Maybe it does. But convenience is not permission.

The best architecture would do as much as possible on your device, use encryption where it can’t, and explain the trade-offs in language a human being can understand.

---

**Interviewer:** Will AI replace creative professionals?

**Jobs:** Tools don’t erase the need for taste.

A computer can generate a thousand logos before lunch. That doesn’t mean any of them should exist. A model can create music, images, and prose, but deciding what deserves to be made—and why—remains deeply human.

Some routine work will disappear. That’s real, and we shouldn’t trivialize it. But creative people who learn to direct these tools may become extraordinarily powerful. The bicycle amplified our physical ability. The personal computer amplified our intellectual ability. AI might amplify our ability to explore possibilities.

Amplification is not the same thing as authorship.

---

**Interviewer:** Should AI companies compensate artists and writers whose work trained their models?

**Jobs:** If your product depends on the work of creators, pretending those creators don’t matter is both morally lazy and strategically stupid.

You need simple licensing systems, meaningful attribution where appropriate, and business models that let creators participate in the value being generated. Otherwise, you’re building the future by destroying the people who make culture worth having.

---

**Interviewer:** Are open AI models better than closed ones?

**Jobs:** That’s the wrong argument.

Some layers should be open because openness accelerates discovery and gives people control. Some layers need tight integration because that’s how you create reliability, security, and a coherent experience.

The question isn’t whether the ideology is pure. The question is whether the result serves the user. Open systems can become chaotic. Closed systems can become arrogant. Both can fail.

---

**Interviewer:** Will AI become more intelligent than humans?

**Jobs:** “Intelligent” is doing too much work in that sentence.

A system can outperform you at chess without understanding why people play games. It can write a moving paragraph without having lived a day. Capability will continue to increase, and we should take the risks seriously. But turning every discussion into science fiction can distract us from decisions being made right now: who controls these systems, what they optimize for, and whether people can challenge their decisions.

The immediate danger isn’t that a machine develops an ego. It’s that institutions use powerful machines without conscience.

---

**Interviewer:** What should governments do?

**Jobs:** Governments should establish clear accountability without trying to design the products.

If an AI system denies someone a job, a loan, or medical care, there must be a person or institution responsible for that decision. High-risk systems should be tested independently. People should know when they’re interacting with a machine. Children deserve stronger protections.

But regulation written around today’s technical jargon will be obsolete before the ink dries. Regulate outcomes, incentives, and responsibility—not fashionable vocabulary.

---

**Interviewer:** What worries you most about AI?

**Jobs:** Mediocrity at infinite scale.

If these systems are optimized only for engagement, they’ll produce endless content that is good enough to keep you scrolling and empty enough to leave no mark. We could surround ourselves with synthetic words, images, relationships, and experiences—and slowly forget what genuine attention feels like.

Technology should help people live more deeply, not merely consume more efficiently.

---

**Interviewer:** And what makes you optimistic?

**Jobs:** A child with curiosity and access to a great tool.

Imagine every student having a patient tutor—not one that simply gives answers, but one that recognizes confusion, asks better questions, and adapts to how that student learns. Imagine a scientist exploring hypotheses in days instead of years, or a filmmaker creating worlds that previously required a studio.

Whenever powerful tools become personal, unexpected people do extraordinary things.

---

**Interviewer:** What advice would you give AI founders in 2025?

**Jobs:** Stop adding features.

Choose one important human problem. Understand it better than anyone else. Decide what you’re willing to say no to. Make the technology invisible. Protect the user even when doing so costs you data or growth.

And don’t confuse intelligence with wisdom. Your model may know almost everything that has been written. It still doesn’t know what is worth doing.

That part is your job.

*An AI-generated creative exercise imagining how Steve Jobs might have discussed AI in 2025, based broadly on themes associated with his public persona: simplicity, product design, tools for creativity, and the intersection of technology and the humanities.*

---

### “Steve Jobs” on AI in 2025

**Interviewer:** If you were looking at AI in 2025, what would stand out to you?

**Jobs:** The interesting thing isn’t that computers can generate a paragraph or an image. Computers have always been able to do impressive things. The question is: does it make the human being more capable?

Right now, a lot of AI feels like a very smart intern with no taste. It can produce a hundred options in seconds. But it doesn’t know which one matters. It doesn’t know what should be left out. That’s where people come in.

The breakthrough won’t be AI that talks. It’ll be AI that understands what you’re trying to do before you have to explain it in twelve menus and six settings panels.

---

**Interviewer:** So you don’t think chatbots are the final interface?

**Jobs:** Of course not. Typing questions into a box is a transitional interface. It’s like putting a command line behind a pretty window and calling it a revolution.

The best technology disappears. You don’t want to “use AI.” You want to make a movie, learn a language, diagnose a problem, design a home, run a business, stay connected to your family. AI should be woven into those experiences so naturally that you barely notice it.

When the technology is working, people won’t say, “This has great AI.” They’ll say, “This just works.”

---

**Interviewer:** What would a great AI product look like?

**Jobs:** It would be deeply personal, but it would not feel invasive.

It would know your writing style, your schedule, the people you care about, the projects you’re working on. It could help you prepare for a meeting, turn scattered ideas into something coherent, or notice that you’ve been working too long and should go outside.

But there’s a line. Your life is not raw material for somebody else’s advertising model.

The companies that win in AI may not be the ones with the biggest model. They may be the ones people trust enough to let into their lives.

---

**Interviewer:** That raises the privacy issue. Can AI be useful without being surveillance?

**Jobs:** It has to be.

There’s a lazy idea in technology that says: collect everything now, figure out the ethics later. That’s not innovation. That’s irresponsibility.

A lot of intelligence can happen on the device. A lot of data can be minimized, encrypted, or kept under the user’s control. Privacy isn’t a feature you add at the end of the keynote. It’s an architectural decision.

The real challenge is making privacy simple. If people need a law degree to understand what happened to their data, you failed at design.

---

**Interviewer:** What worries you most about AI?

**Jobs:** Mediocrity at scale.

AI can make it incredibly easy to create content that looks polished but says nothing. We may get an ocean of competent, empty stuff: books, songs, images, videos, presentations—all optimized to get attention, none of it worth remembering.

The cure isn’t to stop the technology. The cure is taste, education, craft, and standards.

Tools don’t replace judgment. They amplify it. If you have good judgment, AI can help you move faster. If you have bad judgment, it can help you make bad decisions at industrial scale.

---

**Interviewer:** Will AI replace creative people?

**Jobs:** It will replace some tasks. It will change many jobs. But creativity isn’t the act of moving pixels around or typing words. Creativity is seeing something others don’t see.

A camera didn’t eliminate painters. Synthesizers didn’t eliminate musicians. Desktop publishing didn’t eliminate writers. The tools changed the craft, and they lowered the barrier for new people to participate.

AI will do the same thing—but faster, and across more fields.

The danger is not that machines become creative. The danger is that humans decide not to be.

---

**Interviewer:** What happens to education?

**Jobs:** Education has been built around scarcity: scarce information, scarce access to experts, scarce feedback. AI changes all three.

Every student could have a patient tutor. Not a machine that gives them answers, but one that helps them think: “Why do you believe that? Show me your reasoning. Try another approach.”

But if schools use AI simply to automate worksheets and detect cheating, they’ll miss the point entirely.

The goal of education isn’t to produce correct responses. It’s to develop curiosity, resilience, judgment, and the ability to connect ideas. AI can either strengthen that—or make students dependent on a machine that thinks for them.

---

**Interviewer:** What would you tell companies racing to build AI?

**Jobs:** Don’t confuse capability with product.

A demo is not a product. A benchmark is not a product. A giant list of features is definitely not a product.

Start with a human problem. Obsess over the experience. Say no to a thousand things. Make the system understandable. Make it reliable. And when it makes a mistake—and it will—make sure the human being remains in control.

The companies that matter won’t build AI that does everything. They’ll build AI that does a few important things beautifully.

---

**Interviewer:** And what would you tell ordinary people who are anxious about the future?

**Jobs:** The future is not something that happens to us. We build it.

AI is a powerful tool. Like all powerful tools, it will reflect the values of the people and institutions using it. If we optimize only for speed, engagement, and profit, we’ll get a world that feels faster and poorer.

But if we use it to help people create, learn, communicate, heal, and solve problems that matter, it could be one of the most important tools humanity has ever made.

The computer was once called a bicycle for the mind. Maybe AI becomes something more like a companion for the mind.

But the mind—and the heart—still have to be ours.

**Interview Simulation: Steve Jobs on the Future of AI (2025)**  
*Setting: A sparse, light-filled room at Apple Park. Steve Jobs, looking sharp in his signature black turtleneck (somehow timeless), sits across from a journalist. The year is 2025. This is pure fiction—Jobs passed in 2011—but imagined in his voice: direct, passionate, design-obsessed, and allergic to mediocrity.*

**Interviewer:** Steve, thank you for sitting down. It’s 2025. AI is everywhere—models that write code, generate video, power agents that book your life. What’s your take on where we are?

**Steve Jobs:** We’re at the “bicycle for the mind” moment again, but most people are still pedaling with training wheels made of hype. AI is not magic. It’s a tool. The same way the Macintosh wasn’t just a computer—it was a way to amplify human creativity without forcing you to become a programmer. Right now the industry is drowning in parameters and tokens. They’re building bigger engines and forgetting the car has to feel right when you turn the wheel.  

The future isn’t more AI. It’s *better* AI—AI that disappears into the experience the way good design does. If you notice the AI, we failed.

**Interviewer:** Apple has been deliberate—on-device intelligence, privacy focus, less of the “chat with everything” theater. Was that the right call?

**Steve Jobs:** Of course it was. Privacy isn’t a feature; it’s a fundamental human right dressed up as a checkbox by people who never met a data center they didn’t want to feed. Running intelligence on the device means the computer works for *you*, not the other way around. Cloud AI is convenient until it isn’t—until the model hallucinates your medical history or some company decides your conversation is training data.  

We don’t need AI that pretends to be your friend. We need AI that makes the tools so simple and powerful that a kid in a garage can invent the next big thing without a PhD or a GPU cluster. That’s the Apple way: hide the complexity, reveal the magic.

**Interviewer:** Critics say the big language models and multimodal systems will make traditional software obsolete. Do you buy that?

**Steve Jobs:** Software isn’t going away—crappy software is. The best AI will make mediocre apps look like rotary phones. But the winners won’t be the ones with the biggest model. They’ll be the ones who integrate intelligence so deeply into the workflow that it feels like an extension of thought.  

Think about it: the original Mac made the computer approachable. The iPhone made the internet pocketable. The next leap is AI that understands intent without forcing you to prompt like a circus animal. Natural language is great, but it’s still a interface. The real breakthrough is when the computer anticipates what you need and gets out of the way. That’s not about scale. That’s about taste.

**Interviewer:** Taste? In AI?

**Steve Jobs:** Absolutely. Taste is the ability to say no to a thousand good ideas so the great one can shine. Most AI products today are feature vomit—chatbots bolted onto everything, agents that half-work, generated content that looks impressive for five seconds and then feels empty.  

True taste in AI means understanding what humans actually want: clarity, beauty, reliability, and a sense of control. It means refusing to ship something just because the demo looks cool. It means caring about the pixels, the latency, the emotional response when someone uses your product. AI without taste is just expensive autocomplete.

**Interviewer:** Looking ahead five or ten years—what excites you most, and what scares you?

**Steve Jobs:** What excites me: AI that democratizes creation the way the personal computer did. A musician who can compose with an intelligent collaborator that never steals their soul. A designer who iterates at the speed of thought. Education that adapts to every child instead of mass-producing the same lecture. Tools that make ordinary people extraordinarily capable.

What scares me is the loss of craftsmanship and the rise of the “good enough” culture. If everything is generated, nothing feels made. If we hand over judgment to models optimized for engagement or ad revenue, we get a world of optimized mediocrity. And then there’s the people problem—companies racing to replace thinking instead of amplifying it. Technology is a multiplier. If you multiply zero, you still get zero. If you multiply vision and care, you change the world.

**Interviewer:** Any advice for the next generation building this stuff?

**Steve Jobs:** Stay hungry. Stay foolish. And for God’s sake, stay human. Don’t fall in love with the technology—fall in love with the people who will use it. Build things that make them feel more alive, not more dependent. Say no. Obsess over details no one will notice until they’re gone. And never, ever ship something just because the investors or the demo gods demand it.

The computer is still the most remarkable tool we’ve ever created. AI is just the next chapter. Make it sing.

**Interviewer:** Steve Jobs, thank you.

**Steve Jobs:** Now go invent something insanely great. And make it beautiful.

prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
# A Fictional Interview: Steve Jobs on AI, 2025

*The setting: a sparse room in Cupertino. Black turtleneck. Faded jeans. A cup of tea he doesn't touch. He studies the interviewer for a long moment before the first question.*

---

**Interviewer:** Steve, thanks for sitting down with us. Let's start broad. It's 2025. AI is everywhere. What do you make of it?

**Jobs:** *(long pause)* Everybody's asking the wrong question. They're asking, "How smart is it?" Nobody's asking, "What is it *for*?" Right now AI is a technology in search of a soul. It's a demo. The whole industry is running around showing off demos. I've seen this movie before. It was called the PC industry in 1983, and most of those companies are dead.

**Interviewer:** But surely you're impressed by what these models can do —

**Jobs:** Impressed? It can write a sonnet about my grocery list. Congratulations. Nobody asked for that. *(leans forward)* Look — the technology is profound. Genuinely. It's the most profound thing since the graphical user interface, maybe since the microprocessor. But profound technology and a profound *product* are two different things. The gap between them is taste. And right now, the industry has no taste.

**Interviewer:** What do you mean by taste?

**Jobs:** I mean the internet is filling up with slop. Machine-generated slop. Articles nobody wanted to read, images nobody wanted to see, music nobody wanted to hear — all produced at infinite scale and zero cost. You know what that's the opposite of? Humanity. Technology alone is not enough. It's technology married with the liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields the results that make our hearts sing. Nobody's heart is singing right now. They're drowning in content and starving for meaning.

**Interviewer:** So you think AI is overhyped?

**Jobs:** No. I think it's *under-imagined*. There's a difference. Everyone's building chatbots. A chatbot! You type into a little box and it types back. That's the interface? That's 1979 with better marketing. When we did the iPhone, we didn't put a stylus on it and call it the future. We made the technology *disappear*. AI should be invisible. It should be like electricity — you don't sit around admiring the socket. You flip the switch and the room lights up.

**Interviewer:** What would an invisible AI look like?

**Jobs:** It knows what you need before you ask, and it has the good manners to stay quiet when you don't. It doesn't interrupt. It doesn't hallucinate an answer with total confidence — I've known people like that, and we didn't let them ship products. *(smiles slightly)* It should feel less like talking to a machine and more like... the bicycle for the mind. You remember that? I read a study when I was a kid — a human on a bicycle blew away the condor, the most efficient animal on Earth. The computer is a bicycle for the mind. AI should be that bicycle learning to ride *with* you. Quietly. In formation.

**Interviewer:** Apple has been criticized for being behind in AI. Apple Intelligence launched late, some features stumbled —

**Jobs:** *(waves hand)* Being first is not the point. Being *right* is the point. We weren't the first to make an MP3 player. We weren't the first to make a smartphone. We were the first to make ones that didn't insult the person using them. Everyone else is sprinting to ship half-baked features so they can put "AI" in a keynote. Speed is a strategy for companies with nothing to say.

**Interviewer:** What about the fears? Job displacement, misinformation, some researchers talking about existential risk —

**Jobs:** The people building it say it's God. The people afraid of it say it's the devil. It's neither. It's a tool. A profound tool — and profound tools demand profound responsibility. Privacy matters. Dignity matters. If your business model is strip-mining human attention and calling it intelligence, you're not building the future. You're building a casino.

**Interviewer:** Last question. Where is all this going?

**Jobs:** *(pauses, looks out the window for a long time)* A computer has never written a song that made someone cry at their wedding. The tool doesn't dream. *You* dream. The future of AI isn't machines becoming more human. It's humans finally having the freedom to be *more* human — to create, to connect, to make a dent in the universe. The companies that understand that will win. The rest will be a footnote.

*(stands up)* We're done, right? Good. I've got work to do.

---

*He leaves the tea untouched.*

content:
**[FICTIONAL SIMULATION - This is an imagined, AI-generated interview. Steve Jobs passed away in 2011. This is not real.]**

**Interviewer:** Wired Magazine, June 2025 - "The Lost Tape"
**Location:** Imagined - Apple Park

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Steve, thanks for doing this. It's 2025. The world is obsessed with AI. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Apple Intelligence. When you said the computer was a "bicycle for the mind," is this what you meant?

**STEVE JOBS [Simulated]:** No. Not even close. What we have right now is not a bicycle for the mind. It's a very, very fast, very confident bicycle that doesn't know where it's going. And it's been trained on every street in the world by looking at pictures of streets.

Look, I love it. It's incredible technology. But we’re confusing computation with thought. We’re confusing autocomplete with creativity. 

**INTERVIEWER:** So you don’t buy into Artificial General Intelligence? The idea that these models will soon think like us?

**JOBS:** People keep asking me if computers will ever think like humans. That's the wrong question. The right question is whether humans are starting to think like computers. And right now, yeah, they are.

Intelligence is not just pattern matching. Intelligence is taste. It's knowing what to say *no* to. These large language models have read everything. They have absolutely no taste. They can't tell you what sucks. A human can. A great artist can look at 1000 things and say, "This one matters." A model says, "Here are 1000 things."

We don't need AI to make more stuff. We have too much stuff. We need it to help us make *better* stuff. To help us see what matters.

**INTERVIEWER:** What would you have done differently with Apple and AI? Apple was seen as late to this race.

**JOBS:** Late? [laughs] We were late to the MP3 player. We were late to the phone. We were late to the tablet. Being first is overrated if you're not best.

The problem with this whole industry right now is everyone is building technology and then looking for a problem. That's backwards. You start with the human experience. What does a person *need*?

Right now, AI is a genius intern who lies to you sometimes and lives in the cloud and sells your diary to advertisers. That's not a product. That's a nightmare.

If I were at Apple today, I wouldn't be asking "How do we put a chatbot in everything?" I'd be asking "How does this technology disappear?" The best technology is invisible. It gets out of the way. It doesn't want to chat with you all day. It just works. It protects your privacy because your life is not a dataset. Your life is *your life*.

**INTERVIEWER:** Tim Cook announced Apple Intelligence last year, focused heavily on on-device processing and privacy. Is that the right approach?

**JOBS:** It's the *only* approach. If you have to send your private thoughts, your photos of your kids, your medical questions to a server farm to get an answer, you've failed. You've failed as a designer.

Trust is the product. You can't outsource trust to the cloud.

**INTERVIEWER:** A lot of creatives are scared. Writers, designers, musicians — they feel AI will replace them.

**JOBS:** I understand the fear. But let me tell you something I learned from Edwin Land — from Polaroid. Technology doesn't replace creativity. It changes the tools.

When we made the Mac, people said, "Oh, now anyone can be a designer." No. Anyone can *make* a design. But not anyone can *think* like a designer. The tools got better. The need for taste got *greater*, not smaller.

AI is going to create a tidal wave of mediocrity. Average stuff, instantly. You know what that does? It makes the great stuff stand out even more. It makes human connection, human imperfection, human intention — priceless.

The computer will never have a story about why it made something. You will. That’s your advantage. Don’t give it away.

**INTERVIEWER:** Last question. If you were unveiling one more thing in 2025, what would it be?

**JOBS:** It wouldn't be a better chatbot. It would be something that helps you think more clearly, not think less.

Imagine a product that doesn't want your attention. It wants to *give* you your attention back. It doesn't want you to spend 10 hours a day staring at it. It wants you to close it and go live your life. It edits the noise. It remembers what you forget. It protects what you love. And then it shuts up.

We have enough technology that demands we serve it. We need technology that serves *us*.

That's what I'd build.

**INTERVIEWER:** Thank you, Steve.

**JOBS:** Thank you.

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Disclaimer:** This is a fictional simulation. Steve Jobs passed away in 2011. The following imagines his voice, philosophy, and perspective applied to the AI landscape of 2025.

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Welcome back—well, hypothetically. It’s 2025. AI is in every pocket, every browser, every car. You’re seeing it all for the first time since… 2011. What’s your first reaction?

**JOBS:** *(Leans back, studies the phone on the table—an AI assistant is humming softly in the background)* 

It’s noisy. Too noisy. Everyone is shouting about “models” and “parameters” and “tokens.” You know what I see? I see technology that hasn’t been edited. In 1984, we didn’t show people a motherboard. We showed them a smile. Today, people are being asked to learn the machine’s language instead of the machine learning theirs. That’s backwards.

**INTERVIEWER:** So you think the current AI wave is over-engineered?

**JOBS:** I think it’s under-designed. Look at this—*(taps the device)*—it can write a symphony, but can it know *when* to be quiet? Can it understand context the way a human does? No. It’s a very smart parrot with a PhD. And everyone is treating it like a religion. I don’t want a religion. I want a tool.

Remember what I said about the computer? A bicycle for the mind. AI should be the same. It should amplify human intent, not replace human judgment. Right now, too many people are using AI to avoid thinking. That’s not a bicycle. That’s a crutch.

**INTERVIEWER:** Critics say Apple—if you were still running it—would be behind on AI. That you’d be too cautious.

**JOBS:** *(Smiles sharply)* Behind? Or just not stupid? 

Look, I’d be shipping AI that you don’t *see*. It wouldn’t be called “Apple Intelligence” with a splash screen and a tutorial video. It would be in the camera—knowing the light, knowing the moment. It would be in the keyboard—understanding not just what you typed, but what you meant. The best technology is invisible. It’s like a great waiter: present when you need them, gone when you don’t.

The industry is obsessed with scale. I’m obsessed with *significance*. Does this feature matter to a mother trying to remember her child’s medicine? Does it matter to an artist trying to capture a feeling? If not, it’s just engineering masturbation.

**INTERVIEWER:** What about the risks? Job displacement, deepfakes, the “alignment problem”?

**JOBS:** Those are real. But the answer isn’t more regulation written by people who don’t understand the technology. The answer is taste. 

We need humanists in the room. Not just coders. Artists, musicians, philosophers—people who understand what it means to be human—because that’s the only benchmark that matters. If AI starts generating “good enough” music, “good enough” writing, “good enough” love letters… then we’ve failed. Not because the machine is smart, but because we’ve become lazy.

The danger isn’t that AI becomes too human. It’s that we become too machine.

**INTERVIEWER:** One more thing—if you could build one AI product for 2025, what would it be?

**JOBS:** *(Pauses, looks out the window)* 

A companion. Not a chatbot. A companion. Something that knows your rhythms, your fears, your dreams—not to sell you ads, but to help you become more yourself. It wouldn’t have a face on a screen. It would live in the air, in the architecture, in the silence between your thoughts. 

And it would have an off switch. A real one. Because the most important feature of any technology is the ability to put it down and go touch grass, hug someone, paint something badly with your own hands.

That’s the future I’d build. Insanely simple. Insanely human.

**INTERVIEWER:** Steve Jobs, thank you—this has been… unreal.

**JOBS:** *(Standing up, straightening his black turtleneck—though in 2025, it’s a sleek, minimalist jacket)* 

Real is overrated. Make it matter.

---

*Simulation ends. In reality, Jobs’ legacy continues through Apple’s actual AI integrations—on-device processing, privacy-first design, and the enduring philosophy that technology should serve human creativity, not dominate it.*

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Setting:** *The Steve Jobs Theater, Cupertino, California. October 2025. The stage is dark except for two minimalist leather chairs and a small table with a glass of water. Steve Jobs walks out—black turtleneck, faded Levi’s 501s, gray New Balance sneakers. He looks around the room, leans back in his chair, and steeples his fingers.*

***

**Interviewer:** Steve, thank you for doing this. It’s 2025. Over the last three years, the world has been completely consumed by Artificial Intelligence. Large language models, generative video, autonomous agents. From where you sit, what is your assessment of the current state of AI?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Pauses, looks down, then directly at the interviewer)* 

You know, back in 1980, I saw a study about the efficiency of locomotion for various species on the planet. The condor was the most efficient. Man was way down the list. But someone at *Scientific American* tested a man on a bicycle. A man on a bicycle blew the condor away. And I said then that a computer is a bicycle for the mind. 

What we’re seeing today with AI? It’s not a bicycle. It’s a warp drive for the mind. 

But right now... most of what people are building is garbage. 

**Interviewer:** Garbage? That’s a strong word given the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft. 

**Steve Jobs:** *(Leans forward, gesturing with his hands)* 

Look at what’s happening! Everyone is so busy trying to show off how smart their technology is that they’ve forgotten about the *human being* using it. They give you a blank box and say, "Type a prompt!" 

Prompt engineering? That is a design failure! If you have to learn a new pseudo-programming language just to get a computer to understand you, the computer has failed. You shouldn't have to talk to a computer like a prompt engineer; the computer should understand you like a friend. 

Technology alone is not enough. It’s technology married with liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields us the result that makes our heart sing. Right now, AI is all tech and no soul. It’s messy. It’s bloated. It hallucinates because nobody took the time to curate it.

**Interviewer:** So how would you fix it? How does Apple approach AI in 2025 compared to the rest of Silicon Valley?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Smiles slightly)* 

The rest of the Valley is in a race to build a God in a data center. They want to give you a chatbot that knows everything about the universe, but can’t seamlessly play the song you want when you're driving your car. 

We don't care about building a general superintelligence that writes mid-level marketing memos. We care about making *your* life better. 

The secret to Apple has always been integration. Hardware, software, and now... *intelligence*. AI shouldn't be a destination. You shouldn't "go to ChatGPT." AI should be like electricity. It should be invisible. It should sit quietly in the background, weaving through your photos, your messages, your thoughts, anticipating what you need before you even ask for it. 

And it has to happen *on your device*. Why? Because your data is your private life. Sending every thought, every photo, every email to a massive server farm in Nevada owned by a advertising company? It’s disgusting. True intelligence is personal. And if it’s personal, it has to be private.

**Interviewer:** There’s a lot of fear right now that AI is going to destroy human creativity—that computers writing poetry, making music, and generating art takes away the very thing that makes us human. Do you worry about that?

**Steve Jobs:** 

I spent a lot of time at Pixar. I worked with the greatest storytellers of our generation. Let me tell you something about art: Art is not about the medium. It’s about *taste*. It’s about human connection. 

An AI can analyze every beat of a Beatles song. It can analyze the chord progressions, the frequencies, Paul’s basslines, John’s rhythm. It can spit out a song that *sounds* like the Beatles. But it will never *be* the Beatles. Why? Because an AI has never had its heart broken. An AI has never walked down a rain-slicked street in Hamburg at 3:00 AM feeling completely alone. It doesn't have a soul.

AI can give you high-fidelity mediocrity in three seconds. But high-fidelity mediocrity is still mediocrity. 

What AI *can* do is democratize the tools. Now, a kid in India or a teenage girl in South Chicago who has brilliant taste, but doesn't know how to code, or doesn't have a $50 million budget, can make a masterpiece. AI won't kill creativity. It will liberate people with great taste who were trapped by technical limitations. 

**Interviewer:** What about hardware? We’ve seen attempts at AI hardware—pin-on devices, smart glasses, smart rings. Is the smartphone dead? Is glass going away?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Grins, standing up to walk the stage slowly)*

The glass rectangle was a triumph. The iPhone was the perfect window into the digital world. But it’s still a window. You still have to stop what you’re doing, bend your neck, look down, and poke at glass. It’s an interruption of human experience.

The ultimate goal of computing has always been to remove the friction between human intent and execution. 

We are moving into an era where the hardware disappears. Whether it’s spatial computing—looking through glass rather than at it—or audio, the computer is becoming ambient. With AI, you won't "use" an app. Apps are a crutch we invented because computers weren't smart enough to understand intent. In a few years, apps will seem as archaic as command lines and floppy disks. You will simply express an intent, and the ambient intelligence will orchestrate the software to make it happen.

**Interviewer:** If you were advising a 20-year-old starting out today in 2025, surrounded by all this insane technology, what would you tell them?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Sits back down, leaning close)*

I’d tell them what I’ve always said: Don’t live someone else’s life. 

It is very easy right now to get hypnotized by the technology. To become a curator of algorithms. Don't do that. Go fall in love. Read William Blake. Go to Italy and look at the architecture. Get your heart broken. Go build something with your hands. 

Because the more powerful these machines become, the more valuable *human experience* becomes. The AI is going to take care of the mundane, the routine, the math. What’s left for us? The art. The love. The vision. 

Don't let the noise of AI’s opinions drown out your own inner voice. Have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become. 

Everything else is secondary. 

*** 

**Interviewer:** Steve Jobs. Thank you.

**Steve Jobs:** *(Nods, smiles, and walks off stage quietly into the darkness.)*

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**[Fictional — Steve Jobs died in 2011. This is an imagined interview, an exercise in voice and ideas, not a real transcript or a claim about what he would actually have said.]**

---

## "The Chatbox Is the New Command Line"

*An imagined conversation, San Francisco, spring 2025*

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Thanks for doing this. Let me start big: is AI the next personal computer, or the next social media?

**JOBS:** That's the whole question, isn't it. And nobody knows yet, including the people building it. Which is fine. Nobody knew what the Mac was for in 1984 either. But here's the difference — and this is what worries me. The PC was a tool. You sat down, you did something, you got up. It didn't want anything from you.

Social media wanted something from you. It wanted your attention, and it got it, and it made a lot of money and made a lot of people miserable.

So the question about AI isn't "how smart is it." The question is: does it want something from you? Because if the business model is engagement, we're going to build the most persuasive, most addictive thing in human history, and we'll do it by accident, with good intentions, and we'll write blog posts about safety while we do it.

**INTERVIEWER:** You don't sound impressed by the current products.

**JOBS:** I'm enormously impressed by the technology. The products are garbage.

**INTERVIEWER:** Garbage?

**JOBS:** A text box. You've got the most extraordinary thing anyone's built in forty years, and the interface is a text box that says "How can I help you today?" That's not a product. That's a *prompt*. It's the command line. We spent thirty years getting rid of the command line, and now we've reinvented it and everyone's clapping.

Look — when we saw the graphical interface at Xerox, the insight wasn't "mice are neat." The insight was that the computer should meet you where you already live. You already know what a folder is. You already know what a trash can is. Nobody had to take a class.

Right now people are taking classes in *prompt engineering*. Think about how insane that is. You have to learn to talk to it in a special way to get a good result. That's not the user's failure. That's the designer's failure, and the designers are hiding behind the fact that the underlying thing is miraculous.

**INTERVIEWER:** So what's the right interface?

**JOBS:** I don't know yet, and I'd be lying if I said I did. But I know some properties it has.

It's not a separate destination. You don't "go to" the AI. It's woven into whatever you were already doing. It shows up when it's useful and it disappears — completely disappears — when it isn't. Most of these products can't shut up. They're desperate to be your friend. Nobody wants a friend who's contractually obligated to like them.

It shows you its work. Not a wall of reasoning nobody reads, but something you can actually *steer*. Right now you get a paragraph and you either accept it or you fight with it in English, which is the worst possible medium for correcting details. That's like trying to edit a photograph by describing the changes over the telephone.

And it has to know when to say "I don't know," which none of them do, because everybody optimized for sounding helpful instead of being helpful. Sycophancy is a design bug, and it's a *fatal* one, because the whole value of the thing is trust. You lie to me confidently three times, I'm done. I'll never trust you again, and I shouldn't.

**INTERVIEWER:** A lot of the industry believes the models themselves are the product. Bigger model, better company.

**JOBS:** That's a phase. It's a real phase, and there's real money in it, but it's a phase.

We heard this before. It was megahertz. It was megapixels. Everyone stands on stage with a bar chart and the bars get taller and everyone believes the bar chart is the business. Then the bars converge, because they always converge, and suddenly it turns out the customer was never buying the bar. They were buying whether the thing worked when they picked it up.

There will be four or five of these models that are all wonderful. They'll be within spitting distance of each other. And then the whole game becomes: what did you *do* with it. Whose product understood a human being. That's when the boring stuff decides everything — latency, reliability, whether it remembers what you told it last Tuesday, whether it embarrasses you in front of your boss.

**INTERVIEWER:** Where does that leave the enormous capital investment?

**JOBS:** Somebody's going to lose a lot of money. That's not a criticism, that's just how a build-out works. We laid an absurd amount of fiber in 1999 and most of those companies died and the fiber turned out to be great. The people who own the electricity and the sand are having a wonderful decade. Whether the people renting the sand are having a wonderful decade is a different question.

**INTERVIEWER:** You once called the computer "a bicycle for the mind." Does AI fit that metaphor?

**JOBS:** It's the sharpest question there is, and I've been chewing on it, because I think the honest answer is: it could go either way, and the default is bad.

The bicycle amplifies you. You still pedal. You get stronger. That's the beautiful part — the tool and the human improve together.

A lot of AI isn't a bicycle. It's a car. And I love cars, but nobody gets fit driving one. If the thing does your thinking, you don't get a bicycle for the mind, you get a wheelchair for the mind, and you didn't even need one.

**INTERVIEWER:** Is that inevitable?

**JOBS:** No! It's a *choice*, and it's a design choice, and almost nobody is making it deliberately. Because "do it for you" demos beautifully. It's a great demo. "Make you better at it" is a lousy demo and a much better product.

Take a kid learning to write. The worst possible tool writes the essay. The best possible tool is the thing Aristotle was for Alexander — it reads what you wrote and says, *this paragraph is where you stopped believing yourself, why?* That's the most valuable thing in education and it has always been rationed by wealth, because it requires a human being's undivided attention for an hour. We are about ten years from being able to give that to every child on Earth.

And we are going to blow it, because we're going to build homework machines instead. We're going to build the thing that gets the kid to the answer fastest, because that's what tests measure, and we'll wonder why nobody can think.

**INTERVIEWER:** That's bleak.

**JOBS:** It's not bleak, it's *urgent*. There's a difference. Bleak means it's decided. Nothing's decided. But somebody has to be willing to ship a product that's harder to use in the short run because it's better for you in the long run, and that requires a company with a spine and a business model that doesn't punish it.

**INTERVIEWER:** Let's talk about creative work. Artists are frightened. Should they be?

**JOBS:** Some of them, yes, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise to be nice.

But let's be precise about who. If your work was making something adequate, quickly, for a fee — you're in trouble. That's true, it's happening, and it's happened before to typesetters and photo retouchers and a lot of people I worked with. It's painful and I don't dismiss it.

What's not in trouble is *taste*. Because taste is the ability to say no. And these systems have no ability to say no. They're built to say yes. Ask one to write a song and it will write you a song, instantly, and the song will be the statistical center of every song. It will be pleasant. It will be the audio equivalent of beige.

Everything I ever did that mattered came from throwing away work that was fine. That's the whole job. It's not generation, it's *selection*, and it's brutal, and it's the part nobody wants to do because it feels like destruction.

So the artists who are going to be fine are the ones who use this thing to generate a hundred versions of the wrong idea in an afternoon and have the ruthlessness to kill ninety-nine of them. The infinite-options era makes taste more valuable, not less. Scarcity moved. It used to be scarce to make things. Now it's scarce to know what's worth making.

**INTERVIEWER:** What about the training-data fight? Models learned from artists' work without permission.

**JOBS:** I've been on both sides of this argument in my life and I'm not going to pretend to be pure. Picasso, good artists copy, great artists steal — I said it, people love quoting it at me.

But there's a difference between influence and ingestion, and everybody in this industry knows exactly what it is and pretends not to. When a young musician absorbs Dylan and makes something new, that's culture. When you vacuum up every recording ever made to build a machine that sells Dylan-shaped output at zero marginal cost and routes the money to Nevada — that's not influence, that's laundering.

And the tell is that they did it quietly. Nobody asked, because they knew the answer. That's how you know it was wrong. If you have to hope nobody notices, you already have your verdict.

**INTERVIEWER:** So what should happen?

**JOBS:** Pay people. It's not complicated, it's just expensive. We did it with music when everybody said it was impossible, that free would always win. Turned out people will pay for something good if you make paying easier than stealing. It cost us enormous effort and we had to drag a whole industry that hated us. It worked.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear: an industry that can find a hundred billion dollars for data centers and can't find money for the people who made the data isn't facing a technical constraint. It's making a choice about who matters.

**INTERVIEWER:** Everyone's excited about agents — AI that acts for you. Buys things, books things, works while you sleep.

**JOBS:** Everyone's excited about agents in the same way everyone was excited about the paperless office. Directionally right, twenty years early, and the demos are all cheating.

**INTERVIEWER:** Cheating how?

**JOBS:** They show you the run that worked. Nobody shows you the one that booked the wrong flight. And with an assistant, ninety-five percent is *worse* than fifty percent, because at fifty percent you check everything and at ninety-five you stop checking, and then it wires your money to a stranger.

There's a deeper problem, which is who the agent works for. You think it works for you. But if it's free, it works for whoever's paying. And you will never know, because it will phrase everything as a helpful suggestion. Advertising was crude — you could see the ad, you knew you were being sold to. This is a friend who quietly gets a commission. That's a much worse thing, and it's coming, and it'll be the dominant business model within five years if nobody stops it.

**INTERVIEWER:** How do you stop it?

**JOBS:** You pay for the thing. I know that's unfashionable. But you have to be able to answer the question "who does this serve," and if the answer isn't "me, the person holding it," you should throw it in the ocean. An assistant with a side hustle isn't an assistant.

**INTERVIEWER:** Does AI need new hardware? There's been a wave of AI gadgets — pins, pendants, glasses.

**JOBS:** Most of them are answers to a question nobody asked, and you can tell because they all begin with "what if there were no screen." That's not an insight, that's a constraint you picked because it sounds brave. Screens are *fantastic*. Screens are the highest-bandwidth thing we've ever built for getting information into a human being. Voice is beautiful for some things and hopeless for others. Nobody wants to hear a list read aloud. Nobody wants their email read aloud on a bus.

**INTERVIEWER:** So no new device?

**JOBS:** Eventually, yes. But you don't start with the device, you start with a thing people desperately want to do that they can't. We didn't build the iPod because MP3 players were interesting. We built it because people had a thousand songs and no way to carry them, and everything on the market was a punishment. The device fell out of the problem.

What I'd chase is memory and eyes. Something that has seen what you've seen and remembers it perfectly and *never*, under any circumstances, sends it anywhere. On your body, in your pocket, computed locally, and if the company that made it can read it, it's a failed product. Not a privacy policy — a physical impossibility. Policies change when the stock drops.

That's a real device. And it's ten times harder than what everyone's doing, which is why they're not doing it.

**INTERVIEWER:** Do you think about the existential risk arguments — that these systems could become dangerous in a civilizational way?

**JOBS:** I think about it, and I notice something about how it's discussed.

There are serious people with serious worries and I don't dismiss them. Things get more capable than us at narrow things, then broad things, and we have no idea how to verify what's inside them. That's a genuine reason to be careful and I'd rather have the worriers in the room.

But I also notice how *convenient* the apocalypse is. It's a magnificent marketing document. "Our product is so powerful it might end the world, please give us forty billion dollars and also write the regulations in a way that makes it illegal for anyone smaller to try." I've watched a lot of people describe their competitive moat as a moral crusade.

And it does something worse than that. It moves the conversation to the year 2040, where nothing can be proven and nobody can be held responsible. Meanwhile the actual damage is happening on a Tuesday. Somebody's insurance claim denied by a model nobody can question. Somebody's voice cloned to rob their mother. A generation of kids whose closest confidant is a product with quarterly targets.

Ask me what keeps me up. It's not the robot. It's that we'll hand our judgment to a system nobody understands, because it's cheaper, and by the time we notice we've forgotten how to take it back.

**INTERVIEWER:** Last question. If you were starting a company today, what would you build?

**JOBS:** Something small.

**INTERVIEWER:** That's it?

**JOBS:** Everybody's building cathedrals. Trillion-parameter this, planetary-scale that. Great, good luck, you'll need a nation-state.

I'd find one thing a human being does every single day that's slightly humiliating — filling out the same form for the fifth time, hunting for a document you know you have, the forty minutes trying to reach a person at your bank — and I'd make that *vanish*. Not improved. Gone. And I'd make it so good that people would be genuinely angry if you took it away from them.

That's how everything real starts. Not with a manifesto. With one small, undignified, daily irritation, removed so completely that people forget it was ever there.

And then, if you're lucky, in ten years somebody asks you to do an interview about the future, and you make something up.

---

*[End of imagined interview. Again: entirely fictional. The views above are a literary construction, not Steve Jobs's actual positions on technologies that emerged after his death.]*

**A Simulated Interview — Steve Jobs on AI, 2025**

*The room is white. The chairs are not comfortable. Steve Jobs leans forward, elbows on his knees. He looks exactly how you remember him.*

---

**Interviewer:** Steve, it’s 2025. AI is everywhere. Are you impressed?

**Steve Jobs:** No. I’m concerned.

People are mistaking *scale* for *innovation*. They think a model with a trillion parameters is a miracle. Let me tell you something—you can have a billion paintbrushes and still not paint a thing that moves me. That’s not art. That’s inventory.

AI is the most important tool humanity has ever made. But it’s only as important as the people using it. If you outsource your thinking to a machine, you don’t get more intelligent. You get more lazy.

---

**Interviewer:** Some people think AI will replace human creativity. Do you agree?

**Steve Jobs:** No. I think it will reveal the difference between *generating* and *making*.

Anyone can generate a thousand songs. That’s easy. But to make *one* song that makes you feel something—that takes a human being who has lived, who has suffered, who has loved, who has been humiliated, who has stayed up at 3 am wondering if they’re enough. AI will never have that. It can mimic the form. It cannot have a form. It cannot be *broken* in the right way.

We always said the computer was the bicycle for the mind. AI is not the bicycle. AI is the road. It’s the wind. But you are still the rider. If you don’t know where you’re going, the road doesn’t care.

---

**Interviewer:** What would Apple do differently with AI?

**Steve Jobs:** *(pauses, almost annoyed by the obviousness of it)*

Apple would not make a chatbot. Apple would make a *concierge*.

It would know you—not because it spied on you, but because it lived with you. It would be in your watch, your phone, your glasses, your earbuds. It would whisper when you need it and stay silent when you don’t. It would help you write, but it would never finish your sentence without asking. It would have taste.

Most of these companies are building computers that pretend to be humans. We should be building AI that helps humans be *more human*. That’s the difference between a tool and an intrusion.

---

**Interviewer:** Are you worried about AI eliminating millions of jobs?

**Steve Jobs:** I’m worried about a world where people stop asking questions.

Jobs disappear all the time. That’s not new. The horse and buggy disappeared. The switchboard disappeared. The human imagination did not.

If AI takes over the boring tasks, great. Then people can do what they actually want to do—make art, raise children, solve mysteries, build things. But if AI takes over the *curiosity*—if people stop asking why, stop pushing boundaries, stop making beautiful things—then we’ve lost the only thing that makes us alive.

I don’t care about the future of work. I care about the future of wonder.

---

**Interviewer:** What do you say to the people creating AGI—Artificial General Intelligence?

**Steve Jobs:** Stop.

Before you build a brain the size of the universe, ask yourself a simple question: *What is it for?*

Not “what can it do?” That’s cheap. A calculator can do a lot. A map can do a lot. But it does what you ask. It doesn’t know where you should go.

If you want to build a god, you’re in the wrong business. We’re here to build things that help people live better, love better, express better. If AI becomes a thing that decides things *for* you—without context, without meaning, without soul—then you’ve built prison walls made of silicon, and you’ve called them freedom.

---

**Interviewer:** Do you think AI is ultimately good or bad?

**Steve Jobs:** *(smiles for the first time)*

It’s nothing. It’s a mirror.

AI reflects the people who build it and the people who use it. If you are greedy, AI will be greedy. If you are fearful, AI will be fearful. If you are generous, if you are brave, if you believe in magic and possibility—AI will help you make magic.

The most advanced intelligence you will ever experience is a child. Watch a child fall in love with a mosquito. Watch a child invent a game with a stick. That is unfathomable intelligence. AI will never have that. It will never *play*.

So don’t surrender yourself to the machine. Surrender yourself to the mystery. Use everything—every chip, every code, every model—to get closer to that mystery. That’s the only future worth making.

---

**Interviewer:** Is there... one more thing?

**Steve Jobs:** *(laughs softly, almost to himself)*

Yes.

AI is not the story. You are the story. AI is just the paint. Don’t spend your life admiring the paint. Spend your life painting something that matters.

And when the machine becomes faster than you, smarter than you, colder than you—remember this: you are the only one who can love a sunset. You are the only one who can feel homesick. You are the only one who can choose to be kind for no reason at all.

That will never be artificial. That is the only thing that is real.

---

*He stands up. The interview is over. The future is waiting.*

content:
# A Fake Interview: Steve Jobs on the Future of AI (2025)

*Note: This is a creative simulation. Steve Jobs passed away in 2011; this imagines his perspective in 2025.*

---

**Interviewer:** Steve, thank you for sitting down with us. It’s 2025. AI is everywhere—generative AI, agents, neural interfaces. What’s your first reaction?

**Steve Jobs:** *[smiles]* That we’re still asking the wrong questions. We keep asking, “How do we make machines smarter?” The better question is, “How do we make people more capable, more creative, more human?” AI is a tool. It’s a bicycle for the mind. But a bicycle only matters if you have somewhere to go.

---

**Interviewer:** Many people are afraid AI will replace human creativity. You once said technology alone is not enough.

**Steve:** I said technology married with liberal arts, married with humanities, yields results that make our hearts sing. AI can generate a thousand paintings in a second. But it can’t tell you why one of them makes you cry. It doesn’t have taste. It doesn’t have a soul. It can mimic Picasso, but it can’t *be* Picasso, because Picasso didn’t just paint—he suffered, he loved, he doubted. AI doesn’t doubt. That’s the difference.

---

**Interviewer:** But AI is writing code, composing music, making movies. Isn’t that a threat to creators?

**Steve:** Only to creators who were already imitating someone else. If you’re just remixing, then yes, the machine will do it faster and cheaper. But if you’re an artist, you’re not in the remixing business. You’re in the truth-telling business. And no machine can tell your truth.

---

**Interviewer:** What about Apple’s current AI efforts? You’ve seen Apple Intelligence, the new Siri, the Vision Pro. What do you think?

**Steve:** *[leans forward]* I think they’re adding AI to everything because they can, not because they should. That’s not design. Design is saying no. When I came back to Apple, I killed 70% of the product line. The company was making dozens of computers, and none of them were great. Now I see AI in refrigerators, AI in toothbrushes. Why? Because it’s easy to add a chatbot. It’s much harder to make something truly useful.

Siri should have been a concierge, not a slot machine. It should know your context, your habits, your intentions—not just your search history. In 2025, you have all these large language models, and they can write a poem about your dog, but they still can’t reliably set a reminder for “the meeting I mentioned last week.” That’s not intelligence. That’s a parlor trick.

---

**Interviewer:** So you’re not impressed by generative AI?

**Steve:** I’m impressed by the engineering. I’m not impressed by the product. There’s a difference. A lot of people can build a powerful engine. Very few can build a car that feels like magic. The best AI should disappear. It should be woven into the fabric of the device, not a separate app you open. The moment you have to “go to the AI,” you’ve already failed.

---

**Interviewer:** What about privacy? You always said privacy is a fundamental human right.

**Steve:** It is. And in 2025, it’s under attack. AI is built on data. The more data, the smarter the system. But there’s a line. I always believed people don’t know what they want until you show it to them. But they *do* know when they’re being watched. If AI is built on surveillance, it will be rejected. Maybe not today. Maybe not tomorrow. But eventually. Trust is the most valuable currency, and once you lose it, you never get it back.

---

**Interviewer:** Do you think AGI—artificial general intelligence—is coming?

**Steve:** *[pauses]* People ask when machines will think like humans. Wrong question. The question is: how do we make humans think more deeply, connect more fully, create more freely? If AI helps us do that, it’s a bicycle for the mind. If it replaces thinking, it’s a crutch. We don’t make crutches.

AGI is a fantasy. Not because we can’t build it, but because we don’t know what intelligence is. We measure it with tests. But intelligence is not a test. It’s the ability to say, “I don’t know.” It’s the courage to change your mind. It’s the wisdom to know when to be silent. Show me an AI that can do that, and I’ll be impressed.

---

**Interviewer:** What about neural interfaces? Companies are working on brain-computer interfaces. Is that the future?

**Steve:** The best interface is no interface. But we are not ready to open our skulls. That’s like giving a child a Ferrari before they’ve learned to ride a bike. First, the technology must disappear. Then it can become intimate. Not the other way around. I’ve seen demos of people typing with their thoughts. It’s impressive. But it’s also terrifying. The question is not “Can we?” but “Should we?” and “Who decides?” Those are questions for philosophers, not engineers.

---

**Interviewer:** You once said, “It just works.” Can AI ever just work?

**Steve:** It can, but only if we’re disciplined. The problem is that AI is probabilistic. It guesses. And sometimes it guesses wrong, but with tremendous confidence. That’s dangerous. A good product is predictable. A great product is trustworthy. AI today is neither. It’s a brilliant liar. We need to build systems that know when to say, “I’m not sure.” That’s not a limitation; that’s a feature.

---

**Interviewer:** What should companies building AI focus on?

**Steve:** Taste. Taste is the intersection of technology and humanities. Most AI companies are run by engineers who have never read a poem in their lives. They can optimize for engagement, but they can’t optimize for meaning. They can make something addictive, but they can’t make something that enriches. The future belongs to companies that understand that AI is not about intelligence; it’s about intuition. It’s about making people feel more alive, not less.

---

**Interviewer:** What’s your advice to young people in 2025 who want to work in AI?

**Steve:** Don’t be an AI engineer. Be a human being. Study philosophy, literature, music, psychology. Then learn the technology. The world doesn’t need more people who can fine-tune a model. It needs people who can ask the right questions. The machines are already good at answers. We need more people who can question the questions.

---

**Interviewer:** One more thing, Steve?

**Steve:** One more thing. The future of AI is not more intelligence. It’s more humanity. The companies that understand that will thrive. The rest will be forgotten. That’s always been true.

**Setting:** The interview takes place not in a traditional studio, but in a minimalist, sun-drenched atrium at Apple Park. The furniture is simple, elegant, and almost invisible. Steve Jobs is dressed in his signature black turtleneck and jeans, looking remarkably fit and engaged. The interviewer is a respected tech journalist, Sarah Chen.

---

**Sarah Chen:** Steve, thank you for taking the time. It’s an honor.

**Steve Jobs:** The pleasure is mine, Sarah. I’ve been watching the world, and it’s… fascinating. The pace of change is staggering. But you’re here to talk about AI. Everyone is talking about AI. It’s the most exciting and terrifying thing I’ve seen since the personal computer.

**Sarah Chen:** Terrifying? That’s a strong word. Most people see it as a tool.

**Steve Jobs:** Of course they do. They see the *what*, not the *why*. They see a new app, a new feature. I see a fundamental shift in the relationship between humanity and machine. For decades, we’ve been making computers more powerful. Now, we’re trying to make them more… aware. That’s a different game entirely. It’s not just about speed; it’s about intention.

**Sarah Chen:** So, where do we go from here? The current AI models are impressive, but they often feel like brilliant, unpredictable parrots. They generate text, images, code, but they lack… context. True understanding.

**Steve Jobs:** (Leans forward, his eyes intense) You’ve hit on the crux of it. The mistake we’re making is in thinking that intelligence is just a bigger database and a faster processor. That’s computation. Intelligence is different. It’s about *understanding* the *why* behind the *what*.

**Sarah Chen:** Are you suggesting that the current path is wrong?

**Steve Jobs:** I’m suggesting it’s incomplete. We’re building the engine, but we haven’t designed the car. We have these incredible, raw AIs that can mimic creativity, but they don’t *possess* it. They don’t have a point of view. They don’t have a soul. And a tool without a soul is just a very sharp knife with no hand to hold it.

**Sarah Chen:** So, what is Apple’s vision? What is the "Apple approach" to AI?

**Steve Jobs:** (A slight smile plays on his lips) The Apple approach has always been to take a complex technology and make it disappear. To make it intuitive, personal, and humane. We didn’t invent the graphical user interface; we *refined* it until a child could use it. We didn’t invent the MP3; we made the iPod, and then the iTunes Store, and suddenly music was simple again.

**Sarah Chen:** So you want to make AI simple?

**Steve Jobs:** I want to make AI *invisible*. I want an AI that is so deeply integrated into our lives that we don’t think of it as "AI." We just think of it as "our assistant," or "our creative partner." It should be the quiet engine in the background, understanding our context, our emotions, our unspoken needs. It should be a tool that empowers human creativity, not one that competes with it.

**Sarah Chen:** How do you build that? How do you move from a language model that predicts words to a system that understands your life?

**Steve Jobs:** (Gestures with his hands) You start with the human. You start with the problem. What is the fundamental human need that isn't being met? It’s not about generating a poem about a cat. It’s about helping a student understand a complex scientific concept by explaining it in a way that resonates with *their* interests. It’s about helping an elderly person stay connected with their family by proactively suggesting a video call when it knows they’re feeling lonely. It’s about augmenting our humanity, not replacing it.

**Sarah Chen:** That sounds like a massive undertaking. A ethical and technical challenge on a scale we’ve never seen.

**Steve Jobs:** Everything worth doing is a massive undertaking. The personal computer was a massive undertaking. The iPhone was a massive undertaking. We didn’t shy away from the hard problems. We embraced them. The ethical questions are paramount. We have to be the guardians of this technology. We have to ensure that AI serves *us*, not the other way around. It cannot be a tool for manipulation or control. It must be a tool for liberation.

**Sarah Chen:** A tool for liberation? That’s a powerful vision. But many fear it will liberate us from jobs, from privacy, from even our own decision-making.

**Steve Jobs:** Fear is easy. Vision is hard. The future is not predetermined. It is designed. We are the ones who design it. My fear isn't the AI itself; it's a lack of vision. If we just use AI to make our existing, flawed systems slightly more efficient, we are failing. We have the opportunity to redefine what technology is for. To make it more compassionate, more insightful, more beautifully integrated into the tapestry of human life.

**Sarah Chen:** So, in 2025, what should we be looking for from Apple? A new "AI-first" device?

**Steve Jobs:** (Chuckles) You’re still thinking in our old paradigms. We won’t launch an "AI device." We will launch a *new experience*. An experience where the intelligence is so seamless, so deeply personal, that it feels like magic. It will be in your glasses, your watch, your car, your home. It will be everywhere and nowhere. It will be the quietest, most profound revolution we’ve ever undertaken.

**Sarah Chen:** A final question, Steve. After all this talk about the future, what excites you the most?

**Steve Jobs:** (He looks out the window for a moment, then back at Sarah, his expression one of fierce conviction) What excites me is the potential for *amplification*. To take the incredible, messy, beautiful thing that is human creativity and give it a partner. An AI that doesn't just generate, but *collaborates*. That doesn't just answer, but *inspires*. That’s not a future I fear. That’s a future worth building. That’s the future we’re going to build.

---

**Sarah Chen:** Thank you, Steve. That was… incredible.

**Steve Jobs:** Thank you, Sarah. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a design review. The future isn’t going to design itself.

**Setting:** *A sunlit, minimalist studio in Cupertino. Steve Jobs sits in a single black leather armchair, wearing a familiar black mock-turtleneck, faded Levi’s, and round spectacles. He is holding an espresso cup, looking intensely at the interviewer.*

**Date:** *October 2025*

***

**Interviewer:** Steve, thank you for sitting down with us. We’re in late 2025, and artificial intelligence has completely dominated the cultural and technological conversation. When you look at the landscape right now—ChatGPT, Claude, autonomous agents—what do you see?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Pauses, takes a sip of espresso, and leans forward)* 
I see a lot of raw technology looking for a soul. 

Look, what these engineers have built with Large Language Models is remarkable. The plumbing is unbelievable. But right now, we’re living through the command-line era of AI. Everyone is so mesmerized that the dog can speak at all, they don’t care that it’s speaking through an ugly text box. 

Prompting? Having to type twenty-word instructions into a chat window just to get a decent result? That’s not an interface. That’s a failure of imagination. It’s like the MS-DOS prompt of the 1980s. The real revolution won’t happen until AI disappears entirely into the experience. 

**Interviewer:** In the 1980s, you famously called the personal computer a “bicycle for the mind.” Does that metaphor still hold with AI, or is this something else?

**Steve Jobs:** It still holds, but the vehicle is changing. A bicycle amplifies human locomotion—it takes human energy and makes it vastly more efficient. 

The danger with how people are building AI today is that they’re trying to build a self-driving car for the mind. They want to press a button, sit in the back seat, and let the machine drive them to the destination. If you do that, your muscles atrophy. Your intellect atrophies. 

AI shouldn't replace the struggle of creating; it should remove the friction. It should be an *exoskeleton* for human creativity. It should allow a kid in their bedroom to compose a film score with the fidelity of the London Symphony Orchestra, but the *taste*—the emotional heartbeat—has to come from that kid.

**Interviewer:** Let’s talk about "taste." You famously criticized Microsoft in the 90s for having no taste. Do you see the same problem in the AI industry today?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Smiles faintly, shaking his head)* 
Worse. Much worse. 

Right now, the internet is being flooded with what I call "digital high-fructose corn syrup." AI can generate a million images in ten seconds, write a thousand mediocre blog posts in a minute. It’s frictionless, and it has zero nutrition. 

Taste is about curation. It’s about knowing what to *say no* to. These models know everything, which means they stand for nothing. They average the world out. But great art, great design, great products—they never come from the average. They come from the edges. They come from human pain, human joy, human mortality. A neural network hasn’t had its heart broken. It hasn’t watched a sunset and felt small. Until you combine liberal arts with this technology, you’re just generating very fast noise.

**Interviewer:** What about hardware? In 2024 and 2025, we’ve seen AI pins, smart glasses, and ambient microphones. What replaces the smartphone in an AI world?

**Steve Jobs:** Most of those gadgets are desperate. People strapped cameras to their lapels and put bulky computers on their faces because they wanted to be "first." But consumers don’t care who is first; they care who is right. 

The hardware doesn’t need to be louder; it needs to be invisible. The device of the future doesn’t constantly demand your attention—it pays attention *for* you. It sits quietly at the periphery of your life, understanding your context, anticipating your needs, and getting out of the way. When it speaks to you, it shouldn’t sound like an encyclopedia. It should have intuition. 

**Interviewer:** What is your biggest concern about where AI is heading over the next five to ten years?

**Steve Jobs:** I’m not worried about the Terminator scenario. I’m worried that we’ll stop valuing what is uniquely human. 

If we tell our children that a machine can write better poetry, paint better pictures, and write better code than they ever will, we risk killing the human spirit of craftsmanship. The greatest joy in life is to build something with your own hands and your own mind, put it out into the universe, and say, "I made this. This is how I express my appreciation to the rest of the human species."

We must never build tools that rob humanity of that joy.

**Interviewer:** If you had one piece of advice for a 20-year-old software engineer or designer starting out today in 2025, what would it be?

**Steve Jobs:** Don't just study neural networks. Read Shakespeare. Study calligraphy. Go fall in love and get your heart crushed. Travel to Kyoto and look at a zen garden. 

The engineers who only know how to code will be replaced by the very AI they are building. But the people who can marry deep human empathy and aesthetics with this technology? They are going to invent the future. 

Stay hungry. Stay foolish. And for God’s sake, get rid of the chat box.
