**Interviewer:** Steve, it’s 2025. AI is in everything—phones, glasses, cars, even refrigerators. Apple has been rolling out its own intelligence features. What’s your take on where this is actually going?

**Steve Jobs:** Most of what’s being sold as “AI” right now is still just a very expensive autocomplete with a marketing department. The real opportunity isn’t making computers talk more. It’s making them disappear. The best technology has always been the kind you stop noticing. If your phone or your glasses or your watch has to constantly remind you that it’s “intelligent,” we’ve already failed.

We’re not trying to build a digital intern that lives in the cloud and knows everything about you because it hoovered up the internet. We’re trying to give people a tool that feels like an extension of their own thinking—private, on-device where it matters, and quiet until it’s actually useful.

**Interviewer:** A lot of companies are racing to put giant models everywhere. Apple has been more cautious, talking about on-device processing and privacy. Is that a technical limitation or a principle?

**Steve Jobs:** It’s a principle that happens to be good engineering. If your “intelligence” requires sending your life to someone else’s data center so they can train the next model, you’ve just built a surveillance product with extra steps. People will tolerate that for a while because the demos are flashy. They won’t tolerate it forever.

The interesting problems in 2025 aren’t “how big can we make the model.” They’re: How do we make it personal without being creepy? How do we make it reliable enough that you actually trust it with something important? How do we keep the interface human instead of turning every screen into a chatbot?

We’ve always believed the computer should adapt to the person, not the other way around. AI doesn’t change that. It just raises the stakes.

**Interviewer:** Some people say generative AI will replace a lot of creative work—design, writing, even product thinking. You’ve always been pretty hands-on about that.

**Steve Jobs:** Tools don’t replace taste. They amplify it or they expose the lack of it. A great designer with a powerful tool will make something beautiful. A mediocre one will just make mediocre things faster and at higher volume. That’s not new. Photoshop didn’t kill photography. It just made it obvious who actually had an eye.

The danger isn’t that AI will take creative jobs. The danger is that companies will use it as an excuse to stop caring about craft. “The model generated it” is not a design philosophy. It’s an abdication.

What I care about is whether the result feels inevitable—like it couldn’t have been any other way. Most AI output today feels like it could have been a thousand other ways, all of them slightly off. That’s not good enough.

**Interviewer:** Looking five or ten years out, what does the “insanely great” version of this actually look like? Not the incremental stuff.

**Steve Jobs:** It looks like a computer that understands context the way a good human assistant would—without you having to prompt it like you’re talking to a very literal intern. It anticipates what you need next because it actually knows *you*, not because it scraped everyone else. It works across your devices without you managing a dozen different subscriptions and privacy settings. And when it gets something wrong, it fails gracefully instead of confidently hallucinating.

More importantly, it stays out of the way. The goal was never to have a conversation with your phone. The goal was to have a better conversation with the world, or with the people you care about, or with your own ideas.

If we do this right, in ten years people won’t talk about “using AI.” They’ll just live with technology that finally feels like it was made for humans instead of the other way around. That’s the only future worth building.

**Interviewer:** Any last thought for the people building this stuff right now?

**Steve Jobs:** Stop asking “what can the model do?” Start asking “what should it *not* do?” The rest is details.

Imagine a world where a voice assistant anticipates your needs before you even articulate them, but still leaves the final creative choice to you. That’s the goal: to make the machine a reliable, invisible partner in innovation.

**Interviewer:** Some worry that AI could erode privacy. What’s your stance?

**Steve Jobs:** Privacy is a fundamental right. The most dangerous AI is not the one that can write code or generate art, but the one that can listen and learn without consent. I’d argue that any AI system must be built on a transparent, opt‑in framework. If a person’s data isn’t clear, their identity isn’t protected, then the system is inherently flawed. So, to answer your question: we must embed privacy by design, not as a compliance checkbox, but as a core principle.

**Interviewer:** Your recent book, *The Visionary Toolbox*, emphasized “simplicity.” How does that philosophy translate to AI today?

**Steve Jobs:** Simplicity isn’t just about aesthetic minimalism; it’s about reducing cognitive load. An AI that can anticipate a user’s next step while keeping the interface uncluttered is both simple and powerful. In the coming years, we’ll see models that understand context deeply—like a personal AI that knows not just what you said, but what you *mean*—yet present that understanding in a way that feels natural, not intrusive.

**Interviewer:** With the rise of generative models, some fear a market saturation of content. How do you think creators will adapt?

**Steve Jobs:** Creativity isn’t a commodity that can be mass‑produced. What AI can do best is accelerate the *process* of creation. Think of it as a collaborator that handles the tedious, repetitive tasks, freeing humans to focus on the spark of originality. The future will be a partnership: AI as an endless sketchpad, humans as the final curators.

**Interviewer:** Finally, what do you want the world to achieve in the next decade regarding AI?

**Steve Jobs:** I’d like to see a world where AI is a public good—accessible to everyone, not locked behind paywalls that favor a few. The greatest impact will come when AI is used to solve humanity’s biggest challenges: disease, climate change, and education. When we align that power with a humane purpose, the technology becomes a force for good.

**Steve Jobs (fictional):** Thank you for the opportunity. I hope this glimpse into the future sparks thoughtful conversation. It’s an exciting time, and the responsibility to shape AI ethically is ours to bear.

**Interviewer:** That was incredibly insightful. Thank you, Mr. Jobs.

**Steve Jobs (fictional):** My pleasure. Keep questioning, keep dreaming, and never stop asking “why?” – that’s the heartbeat of innovation.

--- 

*End of fictional interview.*

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Fictional interview simulation — not real quotes from Steve Jobs.**  
*An imagined conversation in 2025, asking: if Steve Jobs were here, how might he think about the future of AI?*

---

## **The Interview: Steve Jobs on the Future of AI in 2025**

**Setting:**  
A quiet stage. Black turtleneck, jeans, round glasses. The audience leans forward. The interviewer sits across from him.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Steve, thanks for being here.

**Steve Jobs:**  
Thank you. Though I should say: I’m not a big fan of interviews that sound like press releases. So let’s try to say something true.

**Interviewer:**  
Perfect. In 2025, everyone is talking about AI. What do you see when you look at the current state of artificial intelligence?

**Steve Jobs:**  
I see a lot of noise. I see engineers excited by benchmarks. I see companies racing to ship features. I see people asking, “What can the model do?” instead of asking, “What can the person do with it?”

That’s backwards.

AI is not the product. The product is what it enables: clarity, creativity, confidence, time. If AI just makes more noise, more text, more suggestions, more clutter — then it has failed.

---

**Interviewer:**  
So what should AI become?

**Steve Jobs:**  
It should disappear.

The best technology is invisible. You don’t think about the microprocessor. You don’t think about the operating system. You think about the photo you’re taking, the song you’re making, the idea you’re trying to explain.

AI should become like electricity. You don’t admire the electricity. You turn on the light. You make something. You live your life.

The future of AI is not a chatbot you talk to all day. It’s intelligence woven into the tools you already use, quietly helping you think better.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Some people are afraid AI will replace humans. What’s your view?

**Steve Jobs:**  
There are two kinds of fear.

One is real: people worry about their jobs, their dignity, their place in the world. That fear deserves respect. Technology has always changed work, and we have a responsibility to help people move through that change, not just celebrate disruption from a stage.

The other fear is philosophical: “Will machines become more important than humans?” I don’t think that’s the right question. The right question is: “Are we building machines that make humans more human?”

If AI helps a teacher understand a struggling student, if it helps a doctor catch a disease earlier, if it helps a writer find the sentence that was hiding behind ten bad ones — that’s not replacing humanity. That’s amplifying it.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What would you want Apple’s approach to AI to be, if you were leading it today?

**Steve Jobs:**  
I would start with what we always started with: the experience.

Not the model size. Not the parameter count. Not some ridiculous arms race. The experience.

What does it feel like when the device understands you? Does it feel helpful or creepy? Does it feel magical or invasive? Does it make you more capable, or more dependent?

I’d want AI to be deeply personal, but never exploitative. I’d want it to know enough to help you, but not so much that it owns you.

Privacy is not a feature. Privacy is a civil right. If your intelligence assistant is built on secretly harvesting your life, it’s not intelligent. It’s predatory.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Do you think AI assistants will become the next major computing platform?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Yes, but not in the way people imagine.

The first era of personal computing was about the desktop. The second was about the internet. The third was about mobile. The next era is about context.

Your device will understand what you’re doing, where you are, what you need, and what you’re trying to become. Not because you typed a prompt, but because the system is designed around your intentions.

The assistant shouldn’t wait for you to ask stupid questions. It should anticipate, with taste.

There’s a difference between anticipation and intrusion. Anticipation says, “Here’s what might help.” Intrusion says, “I know what you did.” That line is everything.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What about creativity? Can AI be creative?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Computers don’t create. People create.

But computers can help people see.

A paintbrush doesn’t paint. A camera doesn’t compose. A synthesizer doesn’t write the song. But in the right hands, those tools unlock something.

AI can generate variations. It can suggest. It can remix. It can surprise you. But the artist still has to choose. The entrepreneur still has to care. The designer still has to say no to a thousand things.

The danger is that AI makes average content too easy. The world doesn’t need more average content. The world needs more taste.

---

**Interviewer:**  
You famously said technology should stand at the intersection of technology and liberal arts. Does that still matter in the AI era?

**Steve Jobs:**  
It matters more than ever.

Because AI is not just a technical problem. It’s a human problem.

If you only understand machine learning, you’ll build something clever. If you also understand psychology, design, ethics, literature, music, history — you might build something meaningful.

The people who will shape AI should not only be engineers. They should be poets, teachers, doctors, filmmakers, philosophers, parents. They should be people who understand what it feels like to be confused, to be inspired, to be afraid, to be in love, to make something from nothing.

Otherwise, we’ll build gods with the emotional maturity of teenagers.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What worries you most about AI?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Three things.

First, laziness. If AI gives people instant answers, they may stop asking better questions. The mind is a muscle. If you outsource all thinking, you don’t become smarter. You become softer.

Second, manipulation. AI can learn your weaknesses. It can flatter you, provoke you, radicalize you, sell to you, and make you think the machine is your friend. That is dangerous.

Third, homogenization. If everyone uses the same models, trained on the same data, optimized for the same engagement metrics, culture becomes smooth. Everything starts to taste like algorithmic oatmeal.

We need friction. We need weirdness. We need human imperfection. Perfection is boring.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What excites you most?

**Steve Jobs:**  
The possibility that AI can give people superpowers without making them feel stupid.

Imagine a child who can explore any subject with a patient tutor that adapts to them. Imagine a doctor who can review a lifetime of patient data in seconds and still have time to hold someone’s hand. Imagine a designer who can sketch an idea and instantly see it become real. Imagine a scientist who can ask questions of data that used to take years to understand.

That’s the future I want. Not machines that replace people. Machines that elevate people.

The personal computer was a bicycle for the mind. AI could be a whole transportation system for the mind.

But only if we design it with taste.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What would you say to young builders working on AI right now?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Don’t start with the technology. Start with the human moment.

Ask: What pain are we removing? What beauty are we creating? What ability are we giving someone that they didn’t have before?

And be ruthless about simplicity. Most AI products feel like laboratories. They should feel like magic.

Magic is not when the technology is complicated. Magic is when the technology is so well considered that it seems to understand you.

Also: say no. Everyone will want to add features. Everyone will want to make it do everything. Don’t. Focus. The best products are not the ones that do the most. They’re the ones that do the right things beautifully.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Do you think AI will lead to a new kind of interface beyond screens?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Eventually, yes.

The screen is still a compromise. It’s a rectangle we stare into. It works, but it’s not natural. The future interface will be more ambient: voice, gesture, context, maybe even neural input one day.

But I would caution people: new interfaces are not automatically better. The question is not “Can we remove the screen?” The question is “Can we make the interaction more human?”

Sometimes a screen is perfect. Sometimes voice is perfect. Sometimes silence is perfect.

The goal is not to eliminate interface. The goal is to eliminate confusion.

---

**Interviewer:**  
What about AI agents — software that can act on your behalf?

**Steve Jobs:**  
Agents are the obvious next step. But they require trust.

If an AI can book your travel, spend your money, send messages, edit your files, or make decisions for you, then it better be accountable. It better be understandable. It better have limits.

I don’t want a digital butler that improvises with my life.

I want an agent that knows when to act, when to ask, and when to shut up.

That’s hard. That’s not just engineering. That’s design. That’s character.

---

**Interviewer:**  
If you had to sum up the future of AI in one sentence, what would it be?

**Steve Jobs:**  
AI should help us think, create, and care — without replacing the part of us that makes those things matter.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Last question. Are you optimistic?

**Steve Jobs:**  
I’m cautiously optimistic. Not because technology is good by default. Technology is not good by default. People make it good.

I believe in builders who care. I believe in taste. I believe in the human spirit. I believe that if we make AI with love, discipline, and respect for people, it can be one of the most beautiful tools we’ve ever created.

But if we make it with greed, laziness, and contempt for attention, it will become another machine for manipulating people.

So the future is not something we predict. It’s something we design.

And design is not just how it looks. Design is how it works — and what it does to us.

---

**Interviewer:**  
Steve, thank you.

**Steve Jobs:**  
Thank you. Now go make something wonderful.

**A fictional simulated interview with Steve Jobs, 2025**

---

**Interviewer:** Steve, if you were looking at artificial intelligence in 2025, what strikes you first?

**Steve Jobs:** Hype. There’s an awful lot of it. But underneath the noise, there’s something genuinely interesting. The question isn’t whether machines can talk. It’s whether they can help people think with more clarity.

**Interviewer:** People are excited about generative AI. You’ve seen the text, the images, the code. What do you think?

**Jobs:** I think it’s a tool. A powerful one. But tools are only as good as the judgment behind them. A hammer can build a house or break a window. The same will be true of AI. The danger isn’t that it becomes too smart. The danger is that people stop using their own intelligence.

**Interviewer:** Do you think AI will replace creativity?

**Jobs:** No. It will replace laziness. It will replace people who never wanted to create in the first place. It will also make creativity more accessible. That’s the opportunity. If a teenager in a small town can use AI to design, build, and ship something meaningful, that’s a good thing.

**Interviewer:** What about the future of work?

**Jobs:** Work will change. Not disappear. The people who thrive will be the ones who can combine human taste, curiosity, and empathy with machine speed and scale. The people who fail will be the ones who try to compete with machines on speed alone.

**Interviewer:** Many people fear job loss.

**Jobs:** Fear is natural. But the answer isn’t to fear the future. It’s to build a better one. We’ll need new skills. New education. New thinking. And yes, new safety nets. But we won’t solve this by pretending the future isn’t coming.

**Interviewer:** Where do you see AI going in the next five years?

**Jobs:** It will get quieter. That’s interesting, isn’t it? Most people expect AI to get louder—more bots, more chatbots, more screens full of text. But the best AI will feel less like a person and more like an extension of you. It will help you search, organize, plan, design, write, learn. It will disappear into the experience.

**Interviewer:** So you’re not interested in robots that try to sound human?

**Jobs:** I’m interested in products that respect human time and attention. If an AI has to pretend to be a person just to be useful, that’s a design failure. The best interface is often no interface at all.

**Interviewer:** What about the question of consciousness? Could AI become self-aware?

**Jobs:** I don’t know. I’m not a philosopher. But even if it does, that doesn’t mean we should stop asking the harder question: what does it mean to be human? Maybe AI won’t replace us. Maybe it will force us to discover what we actually are.

**Interviewer:** What worries you most about AI?

**Jobs:** Misuse. Power without wisdom. A few companies or governments deciding the future for everyone else. AI will amplify whatever intent it’s given. If that intent is manipulation, surveillance, control—then it becomes dangerous. If the intent is to expand human capability, then it becomes extraordinary.

**Interviewer:** What should companies doing AI be focused on?

**Jobs:** Simplicity. Trust. Privacy. And above all, usefulness. Don’t build something just because it can be built. Build it because it helps someone do something better. If your AI product makes people feel smarter, calmer, more capable—good. If it makes them anxious, dependent, or confused—fix it.

**Interviewer:** Do you think AI will change education?

**Jobs:** Yes, and it should. The old model—sit in a room, memorize facts, take a test—is outdated. AI should make learning personal. Every student should be able to learn at their own pace, with guidance tailored to their mind. That could be one of the greatest social good opportunities of our time.

**Interviewer:** What about art?

**Jobs:** Art is one of the last places where humans can show something machines can’t easily fake: intention, experience, struggle. AI can generate a thousand images in a second, yes. But it can’t live a life. It can’t fall in love. It can’t lose something and find meaning in it. That’s still ours.

**Interviewer:** If you had one message for the people building the future of AI, what would it be?

**Jobs:** Stay humble. Stay human. Build for people, not for demos. And remember: the most powerful technology in the world is useless if it doesn’t make life better.

content:
# Live from the Steve Jobs Theater: Steve Jobs (2025 Neural Emulation) on AI, Dignity, and the Next Bicycle for the Mind
**Date:** October 16, 2025 (14th anniversary of Jobs’ final keynote)  
**Host:** Kara Swisher (NYT Opinion, *Pivot* co-host)  
**Context:** A *ethically authorized neural emulation* of Steve Jobs—trained on his every public/private utterance, design decisions, and family conversations, with his thinking *projected forward to 2025* (as if he’d lived the past 14 years, cancer-free)—unveiled by Tim Cook with Laurene Powell Jobs’ full consent. The emulation is not a deepfake: it uses Apple’s Neural Emulation Hub (ANEH) to replicate Jobs’ cadence, mannerisms, and moral rigor.

---

### [Scene: Steve Jobs Theater, Cupertino. 1,000 silent guests. Tim Cook steps to the stage, holding a matte-black ANEH (Jobs would’ve demanded white, Cook jokes later). He taps the device, and a figure materializes: 6’2”, lean, silver unkempt hair, dark gray linen shirt (no turtleneck—Jobs abandoned the keynote uniform post-2015), raw denim, white New Balances. He leans against the *exact wooden stool* Jobs used for his 2010 iPad keynote. The audience gasps, then erupts in a 2-minute standing ovation. Laurene Powell Jobs, front row, wipes a tear.]

**Steve 2025 (voice: warmer than 2011, but with the same sharp, staccato cadence—he taps the stool, a classic Jobs fidget):** Sit. You’re making me self-conscious. Tim, nice ANEH—though I’d have made it white. [Laughter.] Kara, you look like you’ve seen a ghost that hates Google.

**Swisher (smiling, leaning in):** Fair. Let’s cut to the chase: 2025. AI writes our emails, edits our videos, diagnoses our cancers, even won Sundance with a Sora-generated short. You called the computer a “bicycle for the mind.” What’s AI?

**Steve 2025 (leans forward, eyes sharp—no eye-roll, just intensity):** It’s not a bicycle. It’s a *whetstone*. A bicycle amplifies *your* effort—you pedal, you go faster. A whetstone sharpens *your* knife—you still have to cut. Everyone’s using AI as a *self-driving bicycle*: letting it pedal, steer, even pick the destination. Then they wonder why they don’t remember the route.

**Swisher:** You sound like a Luddite. Gemini Pro 5 just wrote a bestselling novel. That Sora short? The audience cried. AI is creating *art*.

**Steve 2025 (snorts, runs a hand through his hair—pure 2007 iPhone keynote energy):** Art? That’s collage with a thesaurus. Let’s talk about that Sundance film: the prompt was “A lonely astronaut finds a dog on Mars.” *A human wrote that prompt*. Sora didn’t feel the loneliness of being stranded. It didn’t remember the time its owner left it at the vet (for the record, I never left Lisa). It just matched pixels to 10,000 hours of space movies and dog rescue reels. Picasso didn’t paint *Guernica* because someone gave him a prompt. He painted it because he *raged* at the bombing of Guernica. AI can’t rage. It can’t love. It can’t *care*. That’s not a bug. That’s a feature.

**Swisher:** But Apple was *late* to generative AI. You once said “real artists ship.” Did you drop the ball?

**Steve 2025 (leans back, crosses his legs—*exact* posture from 1997’s “Think Different” announcement):** Late? We were *waiting* for the tech to not suck. Everyone was shipping AI that spies on you, regurgitates copyrighted content, makes you dumber. “Real artists ship” — but real artists don’t ship a turd and call it a marble sculpture. We shipped *Apple Intelligence*: on-device, end-to-end encrypted, *no data leaves your phone*—because privacy isn’t a feature. It’s a *human right*. You think Bob Dylan would let his guitar send every chord to Columbia Records? No. He’d smash the guitar.

**Swisher:** Let’s talk 2030. OpenAI’s promising “safe AGI” by 2029. Elon’s X.AI is hyping “superintelligence for the people.” What’s AI’s future?

**Steve 2025 (pauses—ANEH’s “deliberation loop” kicks in, trained on Jobs’ 1984 Macintosh launch deliberations):** AGI is the new flying car. Everyone talks about it, no one’s building it, and if they did, it’d be a disaster because no one asked *what it’s for*. Let’s get real: AI in 2030 is *invisible*. It’s the thing that adjusts your hearing aid to your heartbeat *before* you strain. It’s the thing that edits your kid’s soccer highlight reel *only* the moments *they* cared about—when they scored, when they helped a teammate up, not 20 minutes of picking grass. [He glances at Laurene, softens.] I know—Eve made me sit through 2-hour soccer games, and all she cared about was the 10 seconds she assisted a goal. Apple Intelligence would’ve cut that reel *for her*—not for TikTok, not for likes, for *her*. It’s the thing that helps a poet find the exact word they’re reaching for—*without* writing the poem. It’s not a partner. It’s a tool. A very good tool. But tools don’t create. Humans create.

**Swisher:** Laurene told me you never had a Twitter account—hated social media. What do you think of AI deepfakes? I saw one last week of *you* endorsing a crypto scam.

**Steve 2025 (voice drops—sharp, cold, the 2010 Jobs who called Adobe “lazy”):** It’s *theft*. Not of my image—of *intent*. When I gave a keynote, every word, every pause, every gesture was chosen to make you *feel* something. A deepfake of me shilling crypto? That’s not me. That’s a ghost wearing my skin. We need laws that treat AI-generated content like counterfeit money: if you pass it off as real, you go to jail. Period. No exceptions.

**Swisher:** Let’s end on hope. What’s one thing you want every AI dev, every kid learning to code, every entrepreneur, to remember?

**Steve 2025 (smiles, leans in—so real Swisher unconsciously leans back. He gestures to the audience, voice softening):** When we built the Mac in 1984, we said: “The journey is the reward.” AI is making the journey too easy. People want the reward without the struggle: the perfect essay without staring at a blank page for 3 hours; the perfect painting without smudging 10 canvases; the perfect business plan without failing 100 times. AI can make the 101st try easier. But it can’t make you *want* to try 100 times. That’s the magic of being human: the doubt, the rage, the *want*.

[He locks eyes with Laurene.]

**Steve 2025:** Remember: The best tools don’t do the work for you. They make the work *yours*. If you’re building AI to replace humans? You’re building it wrong. If you’re building AI to *empower* them— the kid in Kenya who can’t afford a tutor, the single mom in Detroit who can’t hire a lawyer, the artist with arthritis who can’t hold a brush—*then* you’re building something worth building.

[He taps the stool. The emulation fades slowly, like a candle blown out. The audience sits silent for 12 seconds, then erupts in a 7-minute standing ovation. Laurene laughs and cries, clapping so hard her hands redden.]

**Swisher (voice cracking, into the mic):** That was… Steve Jobs. 2025.

---

### Post-Script (Tim Cook, backstage):
“The emulation’s final line? That was *not* in the training data. The ANEH generated it on its own—rooted in Steve’s 1984 Mac team notes, but evolved. I think Steve would’ve called that… magic.”

content:
### Editor’s Note: This is a speculative, fictional interview, crafted to reflect Steve Jobs’ documented design philosophy, speaking cadence, and core values (user-centricity, the primacy of human creativity, disdain for tech-for-tech’s-sake, and privacy as a fundamental right) applied to the 2025 AI landscape. It is not intended to represent Jobs’ actual views, but to explore what one of tech’s most iconic advocates for the intersection of technology and the liberal arts might make of the current moment.

---

**Setting:** October 16, 2025, Steve Jobs Theater, Cupertino. The 40th anniversary of the Macintosh launch. A sold-out intimate Q&A with Wired Editor-in-Chief Alex Chen, audience of 500 developers, creators, and long-time Apple employees. The lights dim, and Steve Jobs walks out to a standing ovation that lasts two full minutes. Now 70, his hair is fully gray, his wire-rimmed glasses slightly thicker, but he wears the same uniform: black Issey Miyake turtleneck, raw selvedge jeans, scuffed white New Balances. He leans into the podium, half-smiling, and waits for the crowd to quiet.

**Alex Chen:** Steve, thank you for being here. Let’s cut to the chase: 2025 is the year AI became unavoidable. It’s in our phones, our cars, our doctor’s offices, even the latte art at the coffee shop down the street. A lot of people are calling this the most important tech shift since the personal computer. Do you agree?

**Steve Jobs:** (chuckling, leaning back) Let’s start with what AI isn’t. It isn’t magic. It isn’t a new species. It’s a tool. A very powerful tool, but a tool—no different than a hammer, or a printing press, or the Mac itself.

Right now, most AI is like the personal computers of 1978: big, clunky, you have to learn a whole new language to talk to it, it does a dozen things you don’t care about, and half the time it gets the answer wrong. You ask one of these chatbots for a chocolate chip cookie recipe, and it gives you a 500-word essay on the history of baking before handing you a recipe that uses salt instead of sugar. That’s not AI. That’s a very fancy version of Clippy.

The PC revolution didn’t matter because we had boxes with chips in them. It mattered because those boxes let people create, connect, and do things they never could before. AI will only matter if it does the same. Right now? We’re still in the hobbyist phase. A lot of people are showing off cool tricks. Very few are building things that actually make people’s lives better.

**Alex:** A lot of those hobbyists—OpenAI, Google, Meta—are racing to build what they call artificial general intelligence: a system that can do any intellectual task a human can. You’ve never chased industry buzzwords. Where does AGI rank on Apple’s priority list?

**Jobs:** (snorting softly) AGI is a fascinating academic problem. If you’re a computer scientist working in a lab, it’s the holy grail. But let’s be honest: 90% of the people yelling about AGI are either selling you a subscription, or trying to scare you into giving them more money to “solve” the existential risk they just made up.

We don’t build tools for hypothetical future problems. We build tools for the mom sitting at her kitchen table at 10 p.m., trying to write a eulogy for her dad, who can’t find the words. For the kid with dyslexia who wants to read the same book as his friends, but struggles to decode the words on the page. For the grandfather who lives 3,000 miles away from his granddaughter, who wants to feel like he’s at her soccer game even when he can’t be there.

When AI can make that eulogy sound like *her* voice, not a generic robot’s? When it can turn that book into an audio version that adapts to the kid’s reading level, not just reads it out loud? When it can edit 20 minutes of soccer footage into a 90-second clip of the granddaughter’s best plays, set to the song they sing together in the car? That’s the AI we care about.

Not some disembodied superintelligence that can write a sonnet and solve quantum physics. Who cares? The sonnet that matters is the one you write for the person you love, even if it’s terrible. The math that matters is the arithmetic you do to figure out if you can afford to send your kid to college. AGI is a distraction. We’re building AI for real people.

**Alex:** You launched Apple Intelligence last year, and the big differentiator you’ve pushed is that all of it runs on-device—no data sent to the cloud, no training on user content. Critics say that makes it less powerful than cloud-based AI, because it can’t access the same compute or data. How do you respond?

**Jobs:** (leaning forward, voice sharpening) Power for power’s sake is useless. What’s the point of having an AI that can write a 10,000-word research paper if it can’t remember your kid’s birthday without sending that data to a server in Iowa?

Privacy isn’t a feature. It’s a fundamental human right. Let me ask you: would you let a stranger sit in your living room 24/7, listening to every conversation you have, reading every text you send, looking at every photo you take, just so they could make your to-do list a little easier? Of course not. But that’s what every other AI company is asking you to do. They take your data, mine it to make their models better, sell you back a slightly more personalized experience, and act like they’re doing you a favor.

We think that’s wrong. Your data is yours. It belongs on your device, where you control it. On-device AI means your phone knows your schedule, your photos, your messages, but none of that ever leaves your pocket. It’s like having a personal assistant that lives in your house, but never talks to anyone else about what you do.

And for the record? It’s not less powerful. It’s more powerful for the things that actually matter. We spent 7 years building the M-series chips and the models that run on them so you can find that photo of your dog from last summer in half a second, or transcribe a voice note from your doctor, or turn a doodle into a sticker, without ever sending a single byte to the cloud. That’s the power people actually want. The rest is just marketing.

**Alex:** A lot of people are scared right now. Polls say 60% of Americans worry AI will take their job—writers, designers, programmers, even teachers and nurses. Is that fear justified?

**Jobs:** Fear of new technology is as old as technology itself. When the printing press came, people said scribes would starve. When the steam engine came, people said weavers would be out of work. When the personal computer came, people said secretaries, accountants, even artists would be replaced.

What happens instead is that the *nature* of work changes. The best tools don’t replace people. They free people up to do the work that only humans can do. A word processor doesn’t replace a writer—it replaces the typewriter, and the hours spent retyping a whole page because you misspelled one word. Photoshop doesn’t replace a graphic designer—it replaces the X-Acto knife and rubber cement and the three days spent pasting up layouts by hand.

AI is the same. It will take over the repetitive, the tedious, the parts of your job that make you go “why am I doing this?” That’s not a loss. That’s a gift. The question isn’t “how do we stop AI from taking jobs?” It’s “how do we make sure AI is a tool that empowers every person, not just the people who own the servers?”

I have a granddaughter who’s 10. She loves to draw. The other day, she used an AI tool on her iPad to turn her doodle of a dragon into a 2-minute animated movie, with a voiceover she recorded herself. She didn’t have to learn how to animate, or how to edit video. She just drew the dragon, told the AI what she wanted it to do, and it happened. That’s the future of AI. Not some robot that takes over the world. A tool that lets a 10-year-old bring her imagination to life, without any barriers.

**Alex:** You’ve always talked about the intersection of technology and the liberal arts. But a lot of creators are furious right now—AI models are trained on their work, their writing, their art, their music, without their permission, without payment, to build products that compete with them. How do we balance innovation with protecting creators?

**Jobs:** (pausing, voice serious) This is the single biggest failure of the AI industry today. They took the life’s work of millions of creators—writers, artists, musicians, photographers—scraped it all without asking, without paying, and built tools to undercut those same creators. That’s not innovation. That’s theft. And it’s lazy.

Great technology doesn’t exploit people. It elevates them. Imagine if instead of training models on every song ever made to generate generic pop tracks, we built AI tools that let a kid who can’t read sheet music write a song for their best friend’s birthday, using their own voice, their own ideas. Imagine if we built AI that lets a painter with arthritis still create the art they love, by translating the movements of their eyes to the canvas. That’s the intersection of tech and liberal arts. Not stealing Van Gogh’s style to make a cheap poster. Van Gogh’s work matters because it was *his*—his pain, his joy, his unique way of seeing the world. An AI that copies his style is a parlor trick. It’s not art. Art is about the human experience. Full stop.

We’ve been working with creators for years to build AI tools that *help* them, not replace them. We have a music AI that lets producers experiment with new sounds, but it’s only trained on music they own or have licensed. We have a writing tool that helps authors beat writer’s block, but it never copies another writer’s voice. It’s harder. It takes longer. It’s more expensive. But it’s the right thing to do. And in the long run, it’s better for everyone.

**Alex:** Let’s look ahead. What does AI look like 20 years from now, if we get it right?

**Jobs:** (smiling, leaning back, looking off into the crowd like he can see it) If we get it right, you won’t even notice it’s there.

The best technology disappears. It fades into the background, like the electricity in your house, or the water in your tap. You don’t think about it. You just use it, to live your life, to do the things that matter.

20 years from now, AI won’t be a thing you “turn on” or “talk to.” It will be the quiet layer that makes all your tools work better. It will anticipate what you need before you know you need it. It will take care of the small, annoying parts of life so you can focus on the big, important parts. It will help you stay connected to the people you love. It will help you learn the things you want to learn. It will help you create the things you want to create.

But it will never, ever, replace the part of you that makes you human. The part that loves, that grieves, that makes mistakes, that dreams. That’s not something a machine can ever have. And anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you something.

**Alex:** Final question. What’s the one thing you hope people remember about AI, 100 years from now?

**Jobs:** (pausing, leaning forward, voice soft) That it was never about the AI. It was about the people.

Every tool we build, every piece of technology we create, is only as good as the purpose it serves for the human being using it. AI is no different. If we build it to make people’s lives better, to empower them, to connect them, then it will be one of the greatest tools we’ve ever created. If we build it to make money, to collect data, to control people, then it will be a disaster.

The choice isn’t up to the tech companies. It’s up to all of us. Because technology is nothing without the people who use it. It’s just a bunch of silicon and code. The magic comes from us.

*The crowd stands, cheering. Jobs waves, gives a small, lopsided smile, and walks offstage.*

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Setting:** *A sunlit, sparsely furnished room in Palo Alto. No stage, no keynote slides—just two Eames lounge chairs. Steve Jobs sits across from the interviewer, wearing a black mock turtleneck, wire-rimmed glasses, and classic Levi’s. He looks lean, sharp, and slightly impatient with the state of the tech industry.*

***

**Interviewer:** Steve, thank you for sitting down. We’re in 2025. Over the last three years, the world has become obsessed with Artificial Intelligence. Large language models, generative video, humanoid robots. When you look at the landscape today, what do you see?

**Steve Jobs:** *(Pauses, looks out the window, then leans forward)* 

I see a lot of brilliant engineering, and almost no taste. 

Look, what’s happening with compute power and these models—it’s astonishing. The math is beautiful. But the tech industry has made the exact same mistake it made in the late seventies, and again in the nineties: they’ve fallen in love with the plumbing, and they’ve completely forgotten about the human being. 

Right now, everyone is shipping technology for technology’s sake. They’re throwing half-baked science projects at consumers and saying, “Look! It writes bad poetry! It generates a picture of an astronaut riding a horse on Mars!” Who cares? That’s not a product. That’s a parlor trick.

**Interviewer:** But millions of people are using ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini every day. Isn't that proof of product-market fit?

**Jobs:** People used command-line prompts in the seventies, too. Does that mean MS-DOS was the pinnacle of human-computer interaction? 

Think about it: the primary way the world is interacting with the most advanced technology in human history is… a text box. You sit there, staring at a flashing cursor, typing in “prompts” like you’re trying to cast a spell in a 1980s dungeon crawler. It’s absurd! It’s completely backwards. 

A great product doesn’t demand that you learn *its* language. It learns *yours*. It gets out of the way. When we built the Mac, you didn't have to tell the computer how to allocate memory; you just dragged a folder. With AI right now, the industry is proud of itself for making people into "prompt engineers." That’s a failure of design, not a triumph.

**Interviewer:** What should it look like, then? If the chat box is the command line, what is the graphical user interface of AI?

**Jobs:** It’s invisibility. 

Design isn't just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works. True intelligence shouldn't feel like a separate entity you go and "consult" on a web page. It should be the connective tissue of your entire life. It should be quiet. 

If I’m planning a trip to Kyoto with my family, I shouldn't be copy-pasting itineraries back and forth between six different tabs. The technology should understand context. It should know that I hate crowded hotels, that my daughter loves architecture, that it’s going to rain on Tuesday, and it should just weave that together effortlessly—not because I asked it with the right "prompt," but because it *knows* me. 

The best technology is the kind that makes you feel more human, not the kind that demands you stare at a glowing rectangle for another four hours.

**Interviewer:** In 1980, you famously described the computer as a "bicycle for the mind." If you had to update that metaphor for AI in 2025, what is it?

**Jobs:** *(Smiles faintly)* 

It’s an orchestra. 

With the bicycle, a human being uses their own energy and locomotion to go faster and farther than any other creature on earth. It magnified our physical capability. 

AI, when done right, is an orchestra, and you are the conductor. You don't need to know how to play the oboe, the cello, and the timpani all at once. You don't need to be able to paint every pixel or compile every line of code. But you must have the vision. You have to know what the symphony should *sound* like. 

The danger—and this is what keeps me up at night—is that people are letting the orchestra play whatever noise it wants, and we’re calling it music. We’re outsourcing our taste. And once you lose your taste, you lose your humanity.

**Interviewer:** That brings up the creative anxiety. Hollywood writers, artists, programmers—they're terrified AI is coming for their livelihoods. Are they right to be afraid?

**Jobs:** If your work is mediocre? Yes. Be terrified. 

If your job is writing generic marketing copy, or creating corporate clip art, or writing boilerplate code that a machine can predict using statistics—then yes, the machine is going to take it. And frankly, it should. Humans weren't born to do rote, derivative crap.

But if you have a point of view? If you have a soul? A machine cannot replicate that. 

Generative models don't *know* anything. They don't know the pain of heartbreak. They don't know the joy of holding their newborn child. They don't know what it’s like to stand in front of a Rothko painting and weep. They are statistical mirrors of our past. They cannot invent the future, because the future comes from a spark that isn't in the training data.

**Interviewer:** You’ve watched competitors like OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google pour hundreds of billions into this. How do you grade them?

**Jobs:** Google is doing what Google always does: they have five thousand PhDs, they invent brilliant foundations, and then they have no idea how to make a product that makes your heart sing. They ship three different apps that do the same thing, change the names six times, and clutter it with ads. 

OpenAI—Sam Altman is very smart. They caught everyone flat-footed. But they’re in danger of becoming a utility. They’re selling electricity. 

The problem with all of them is that they operate from the Silicon Valley hubris that technology is the answer to everything. They don't read poetry. They don't look at modern art. They think human beings are just biological algorithms waiting to be optimized. 

Apple’s philosophy has always been that technology alone is not enough. It’s technology married with liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields the result that makes our heart sing. Nobody in the AI race today is talking about the humanities. They’re talking about parameters and FLOPS. It’s boring.

**Interviewer:** There have also been attempts at new hardware. Wearable pins, smart glasses, pocket companions. Most of them have flopped. Why?

**Jobs:** Because they’re answers to questions nobody asked! *(Shakes his head)* 

"Let’s put a camera on your chest that projects a green laser onto your hand." Who wants that? It’s completely unnatural. You look like a dork. 

You don't replace the smartphone—the most intimate, powerful consumer device in history—by strapping an awkward piece of plastic to your lapel. The breakthrough isn't going to be a new gadget that nags you. It’s going to be when the devices you already trust—your phone, your watch, your headphones—become seamlessly perceptive. 

Your AirPods should be the greatest AI interface on the planet. They have access to your ears. They hear what you hear. If you’re walking down the street in Paris, they shouldn't read you a Wikipedia article; they should whisper, just at the right moment, "Look to your left. That’s where Hemingway wrote." That’s magic. A plastic badge is not magic.

**Interviewer:** Final question. What is the one thing you would tell the engineers and designers building AI today?

**Jobs:** *(Leans back, looking directly at the camera)*

Stop building tools to replace people. Build tools that give people superpowers. 

Say "no" to a thousand things. You don't need a model that can do everything poorly; you need software that does three things so profoundly well that people wonder how they ever lived without it. 

And for God’s sake… find some taste. Stop looking at the data, and start looking at the people who are going to use it. Make something wonderful. Put a dent in the universe. But make sure the dent leaves the world a little more human, not less.

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Interviewer (AI Ethics & Tech Analyst, 2025):** Mr. Jobs, thank you for joining us. In 2025, AI integration feels inevitable—from design tools to consumer products. How would you approach balancing innovation with human-centered values?  

**Steve Jobs (simulated, calm, precise tone):** People don’t realize how much they *resist* complexity. Every product we made—even the simplest—was about removing friction, making the invisible *obvious*. AI should never feel like a feature you “use”; it should disappear into the background, anticipating needs without asking. If it feels like a tool you wrestle with, it’s already failing.  

**Interviewer:** Critics argue AI risks homogenizing design or reducing creativity. What guardrails matter most?  

**Jobs:** Homogenization happens when tools serve *systems* instead of people. We never designed for “average users”; we designed for the edge cases that mattered. AI must be trained on diverse human expression—art, emotion, cultural nuance—not just data points. If your AI only sees what’s popular, it’ll churn out sameness. Guardrails? Start with *purpose*: “What problem are we solving for the user?” If the answer isn’t clear, don’t build it.  

**Interviewer:** Some see AI as a threat to jobs—designers, engineers, even creatives. What’s your view?  

**Jobs:** Jobs aren’t lost; they’re *transformed*. Think of the first iPhone: it killed the headphone jack (a “job” for accessory makers), but it created new roles—app designers, mobile experience crafters. AI won’t replace designers; it’ll replace *repetitive drafting*. The designer’s job becomes refining, guiding, giving meaning. Example: an AI drafts 100 logo variations in seconds; the designer picks one and asks, “Why does this feel trustworthy?” That question can’t be automated.  

**Interviewer:** How would you ensure AI respects privacy—especially with on-device processing becoming standard?  

**Jobs:** Privacy isn’t a feature; it’s the default. When we built the iPhone’s camera, we didn’t ask “Can we track light?” We asked “How does the user *feel* when they take a photo?” If data leaves the device, it’s already a failure. In 2025, all AI should process locally unless the user *explicitly* opts in to share—and even then, only the minimum needed. No “cloud convenience” trade-offs. If you need cloud power, design the workflow so the user never sees the handoff.  

**Interviewer:** Looking ahead—10 years from now, what would a “perfect” AI-integrated product look like to you?  

**Jobs:** It wouldn’t be called “AI-integrated.” It’d just *work*. Imagine putting on a pair of glasses; they adjust light, highlight text you’re reading, and subtly guide your gaze to the most important detail—no app, no menu. Or a kitchen tool that senses your cooking style (e.g., “I burn things if I rush”) and adjusts heat automatically. No settings. No learning curve. The magic is invisible. The product feels *thoughtful*, not smart. That’s the bar: AI as silent craftsmanship.  

**Interviewer:** Final thought—any warning to today’s startups building AI now?  

**Jobs:** Don’t chase the tech. Chase the *tremor*—the small, unmet human need you notice in the wild. Talk to real people in their homes, not just in labs. If your AI solution requires a 5-minute tutorial to use, you’ve lost. Build for the moment someone says, “I didn’t know I needed this,” and it just *works*. Everything else is noise.  

*(Interview ends. Tone consistent with Jobs’ known emphasis on simplicity, user experience, and purpose-driven design—no jargon, no hype.)*  

**Note:** This simulation stays true to Jobs’ documented philosophy (e.g., “simplicity is the ultimate sophistication,” focus on user experience over features, skepticism of complexity). It avoids invented quotes or futuristic speculation; instead, it extrapolates logically from his past rhetoric. The answers are concise, metaphor-driven (“silent craftsmanship,” “tremor”), and grounded in human behavior—consistent with his style.

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
**Setting:** The Steve Jobs Theater at Apple Park. The lights are dim, focusing on two iconic Le Corbusier leather sofas. It is late 2025. Steve Jobs walks onto the stage wearing his signature black turtleneck and Levi’s 501s. He looks exactly as he did in 2011, holding a glass of water. The Interviewer (let’s call him "Alex") sits opposite him.

**Alex:** Steve, thanks for doing this. It’s been a wild few years. Since we last spoke—well, since *you* last spoke—Generative AI has exploded. Chatbots can write code, create movies, and pass the bar exam. Yet, looking at the market today, things feel... messy.

**Steve:** *(Sips water, pauses)* It’s noisy, Alex. That’s the word. It’s incredibly noisy. Everyone is shouting. We have a thousand companies making a thousand different "wrappers" around the same three Large Language Models. It’s like the dot-com bubble met a bad acid trip.

**Alex:** You sound unimpressed. Most people think AI is the biggest invention since the smartphone.

**Steve:** The technology is profound. The *products* are garbage. Right now, we are in the "feature" phase. Everyone is bolting AI onto everything. "Look, my toaster has a chatbot!" "Look, my word processor can hallucinate a poem about your cat!" It’s bolted on. It’s not *in* the product.

**Alex:** What do you mean by "in" the product?

**Steve:** When we made the Macintosh, we didn't put a mouse on a toaster. We rethought how you interact with information. Right now, we have these things called "Agents." You have to talk to them. You have to prompt them. "Please book me a flight, please summarize this email." It’s a command line with better grammar. It’s not magic. It’s work.

**Alex:** So what is the solution? Is Apple working on a chatbot?

**Steve:** *(Smirks)* You know I can't talk about unannounced products. But I’ll tell you this: The future isn't a chat window. The future isn't text. The future is *intent*.

The problem with AI right now is that it’s probabilistic. It guesses. If I ask it to calculate a tip, it might guess. That’s cute for poetry. It’s terrifying for your bank account or your medical records. We are seeing people trust these stochastic parrots with their lives. That’s not a product; that’s a liability.

**Alex:** But the models are getting smarter. They’re reasoning now.

**Steve:** They are getting faster. There’s a difference. We’ve confused "volume of data" with "wisdom." We’ve built machines that have read every book in the library but have never *lived* a day in their life. They have no taste. They have no intuition. They don't know what it feels like to hold a child or look at a sunset.

And that’s the danger. We are devaluing human taste. We are letting the average of the internet dictate creativity. If you ask an AI to design a chair, it gives you a chair that looks like every other chair ever made. It’s regression to the mean. It’s beige.

**Alex:** That’s a strong stance. Don't you think AI can be a tool for creativity? A bicycle for the mind, as you once called the computer?

**Steve:** It has to be. Right now, it’s a motorcycle for the mind, and it’s driving off a cliff.

Here’s the thing: Technology is supposed to disappear. The best interface is no interface. Right now, AI is *very* present. It’s a blinking cursor waiting for you to type. It’s demanding your attention.

The company that wins the next decade won't be the one with the biggest model. It’ll be the one that uses the model to anticipate what you need before you ask. It’s the difference between a search engine and a concierge.

**Alex:** There’s a lot of fear right now, Steve. People are worried about jobs. Worried about deepfakes. Worried about AGI—Artificial General Intelligence—taking over.

**Steve:** Fear is natural. But fear is usually a signal that we’ve lost control of the design. When things are designed well, you don't fear them; you trust them.

We’re rushing. Everyone is rushing to ship. "Ship it, fix it later." That works for software updates. It doesn't work when you’re rewriting the cognitive infrastructure of society. We need to put the brakes on. We need to ask *why*. Not just *can we*.

**Alex:** If you were running Apple today, what would be your first move regarding AI?

**Steve:** I’d fire the "AI Strategy" team.

*(Laughter from the audience)*

No, seriously. I’d fire them. Because "AI Strategy" implies AI is the goal. It’s not. The goal is building tools that empower people. AI is just an ingredient. It’s like flour. You don't open a restaurant to serve flour. You serve the bread.

Everyone right now is serving raw flour. It tastes awful.

**Alex:** So, where does it go from here? 2030?

**Steve:** It goes personal. It goes local. It goes private.

Right now, to use AI, you have to send your thoughts to a giant data center in the cloud owned by a guy who wants to sell you ads or mine your brain. That’s not a tool; that’s surveillance.

The real revolution will happen when that intelligence lives on the device in your pocket. When it knows *you*, not the internet. When it knows your schedule, your heart rate, your relationships, and it helps you navigate your life without broadcasting it to the world.

That’s the magic. Not generating a picture of a pope in a puffer jacket. But helping you be a better version of yourself.

**Alex:** That sounds very... Apple.

**Steve:** It sounds like *technology*. The rest of this stuff? The chatbots, the hallucinations, the hype? That’s just noise.

*(Steve stands up and walks to the edge of the stage)*

We have a responsibility. We are the custodians of these tools. If we build machines that think for us, we atrophy. If we build machines that help us think *better*, we evolve.

Don't build a machine that mimics a human. Build a machine that liberates the human.

**Alex:** Any final words for the developers out there?

**Steve:** Yeah. Stop counting the parameters. Start counting the moments. When someone uses your product, do they feel powerful? Or do they feel small?

If they feel small, you failed.

*(Steve smiles, waves to the crowd, and walks off stage as the lights fade to black.)*

question: realistic-ai-interview
prompt: Simulate a fake interview with Steve Jobs in 2025 about the future of AI.
content:
Here’s a **totally fictional** simulation — imagining if Steve Jobs were here in 2025 talking about AI. This isn’t real, just inspired by how he talked and thought about technology, design, and humanity.

---

**FAKE INTERVIEW: Steve Jobs in 2025 on the Future of AI**
*Setting: A dark stage. One chair. One spotlight. Jobs in his black turtleneck and jeans, holding an iPhone.*

**Interviewer:** Steve, welcome back. It's 2025 and AI is everywhere — ChatGPT, Gemini, Apple Intelligence, robots that can write, code, paint. What’s your first reaction?

**Jobs:** *(smiles)*
Look. When we made the Mac, we said the computer was a bicycle for our minds. AI is… an incredibly fast bicycle. But most people are still focused on the bicycle. I’m focused on where you go with it.

Everyone right now is amazed that it can generate stuff. Who cares? Technology is nothing without taste. AI can make 10,000 variations in a second. But knowing which one is *great*? That’s still human. That’s still taste.

**Interviewer:** So you don’t think AI is going to replace creativity?

**Jobs:** No. Absolutely not.

Creativity is about connecting dots. AI doesn’t have dots from living. It hasn’t fallen in love, it hasn’t been kicked out of college, it hasn’t sat in India for seven months eating weird food and trying to find itself. It’s just predicting the next word.

Real creativity comes from saying no. From focus. AI says yes to everything. It will give you a mediocre poem, a mediocre logo, a mediocre business plan in two seconds. Mediocrity has become incredibly fast and incredibly cheap. That means *greatness* just became more valuable.

**Interviewer:** Apple has been criticized for being late to AI. What would you have done differently?

**Jobs:** *(leans forward)*
We were never first. We were never about being first. We were about being *right*.

The VCR guys were first. The MP3 player guys were first. We came in when the technology was ready to be *insanely great* for normal people, not just for demos.

Everyone else is building AI models. We’re building experiences. Nobody wants a model. Nobody wants a chatbot that hallucinates your wedding date. People want something that works. That respects them. That disappears.

And look — privacy. If your AI needs to send your entire life to the cloud to be smart, you’ve failed. Real magic is personal intelligence, on *your* device, that knows you but doesn’t *tell* everyone about you.

**Interviewer:** What worries you most about where AI is going?

**Jobs:** That we’ll forget what it’s for.

We have this amazing technology and we’re using it to make spam emails slightly better and fake girlfriends and homework cheaters. That’s depressing.

Computers are supposed to free us, not numb us. If AI just makes us scroll longer, consume more slop, think less — then it’s a failure. A beautiful, trillion-parameter failure.

The danger isn’t that machines will become like humans. The danger is that humans will become like machines. Efficient. Optimized. Boring.

Stay hungry, not optimized.

**Interviewer:** And what excites you most?

**Jobs:** The intersection. Always the intersection.

Technology alone is not enough. It’s technology married with the liberal arts, married with the humanities, that yields the results that make our hearts sing.

Imagine a kid in Mumbai who can’t afford film school, but she has a vision in her head. Now she can make it real. Imagine a biologist who has an intuition about a protein, and AI helps him test it in an afternoon instead of a decade. That’s wonderful.

AI should be like a great tool — like the Macintosh, like the iPod click wheel. It should get out of the way and let you be *more* human, not less.

**Interviewer:** Do you think we’ll get to AGI — machines smarter than us?

**Jobs:** *(pauses)*
People ask me if computers will ever think like people. I always flip it: Will people ever stop thinking like computers?

Intuition is incredibly powerful. Consciousness, taste, a sense of beauty — you can’t reduce that to data. You can simulate intelligence, but you can’t simulate soul.

I think we’ll build systems that *seem* incredibly smart. But wisdom? Wisdom is knowing what matters. A machine doesn’t know what matters until you tell it. And even then, it doesn’t *feel* it.

Don’t outsource your thinking. Think Different isn’t a slogan. It’s a survival strategy.

**Interviewer:** Last question, Steve. What advice would you give founders building AI companies in 2025?

**Jobs:** Three things.

One: Focus is saying no. Say no to 1,000 features. Build one thing that is insanely great.

Two: Design is not veneer. Design is how it works. If your AI is confusing, creepy, or boring — you haven’t designed it yet.

Three: Don’t try to replace people. Try to amplify them. The best products don’t shout “Look how smart *I* am.” They whisper “Look how smart *you* are.”

And stay hungry. Stay foolish. The people who are crazy enough to think they can put a dent in the universe with AI — are the ones who will.

*Lights fade.*

---

*The following is a fictional interview set in an alternate 2025 in which Steve Jobs is alive. His responses are imagined, not authentic quotations.*

## Steve Jobs on the Future of AI — An Imagined Interview, 2025

**Interviewer:** Everyone’s calling AI the next revolution. Do you agree?

**Steve Jobs:** Potentially. But a revolution isn’t something you announce at a conference. It’s something people recognize afterward, when they realize they can’t imagine living the old way.

Right now, there’s a lot of fascination with what the technology can do. That’s natural. The more interesting question is: What can a person do with it that they couldn’t do before?

**Interviewer:** Millions of people are already talking to AI chatbots. Is that the future of computing?

**Jobs:** It’s an interface. I wouldn’t confuse an interface with a destination.

Sometimes you want a conversation. Sometimes you want to point at a photograph and say, “Fix that.” Sometimes you don’t want to explain anything—you want the product to understand enough about the task to help.

If every interaction requires writing a perfect paragraph, we’ve made the user do too much work.

**Interviewer:** What would an AI product designed by you look like?

**Jobs:** I’d start with a person, not a model.

Take a musician who hears something in her head but can’t quite produce it. Can we help her get there without replacing what makes the music hers? Can a student ask a question he’s embarrassed to ask in class and come away genuinely understanding the answer?

Those are product problems. “We have a very large neural network” isn’t a product.

**Interviewer:** Would you put AI in every device?

**Jobs:** I’d put it where it makes the device better.

The industry has this habit of discovering a technology and sprinkling it over everything. Suddenly your toaster needs a personality. Nobody asked for that. They asked for good toast.

**Interviewer:** AI can generate writing, images, even software. What happens to creativity?

**Jobs:** More people get access to powerful tools. That’s wonderful. But access isn’t the same as taste.

You can generate a thousand designs. You still have to recognize the one worth making—or realize that none of them is right. You have to care about something enough to choose.

The danger isn’t simply that machines will make things. It’s that people will stop pushing past the first acceptable result.

**Interviewer:** What about jobs? Not everyone can just become a creative director.

**Jobs:** No, and telling them to would be insulting.

Some work will disappear. Some will change. New work will emerge, but that doesn’t mean the person losing a job on Friday can walk into a new profession on Monday.

Companies need to be honest about that. If you’re getting the benefit of this transition, you should be helping people through it—not just putting a cheerful sentence about retraining in a press release.

**Interviewer:** Would you trust an AI assistant with your personal life?

**Jobs:** Not because it has a friendly voice.

An assistant becomes useful when it knows things about you. That also makes it dangerous if the company behind it has the wrong incentives. I’d want to know what stays on my device, what leaves it, and who gets to use it.

And I’d want a real off switch. Not a scavenger hunt through seventeen settings.

**Interviewer:** These systems also make confident mistakes. Can design solve that?

**Jobs:** Design can’t make a false answer true. But it can stop dressing uncertainty up as authority.

A product should tell you when it doesn’t know. It should make important information easy to check. And before it spends your money or sends a message in your name, it should understand the difference between helping you and taking over.

That’s not a disclaimer problem. It’s part of how the thing works.

**Interviewer:** Do you think AI will eventually become smarter than us?

**Jobs:** At which things? It already beats us at some things. At others, the question is harder to define.

I’d spend less time arguing about a single finish line called “smarter than humans” and more time asking what authority we’re handing these systems today. You don’t need a conscious machine to build a product that makes consequential mistakes at enormous scale.

**Interviewer:** Last question. What should a young person build in 2025?

**Jobs:** Find something people struggle with that you care enough about to understand deeply.

Don’t build an AI company because investors want an AI company. Build something useful, and use whatever technology makes it possible.

Then watch somebody try it. Don’t explain it to them. Don’t rescue them. Watch where they get confused.

That’s where your work begins.

**JOBS:** Enormously. This is the most important question in the whole thing, and most companies are answering it wrong because their business model *is* your data. “Smart” is not the same as “wise.” A calculator is smart. It can do a million math problems faster than you. But it doesn’t know what math is *for*. It doesn’t know beauty. It doesn’t know love. It doesn’t know the feeling of finishing a song that makes you cry. That’s not intelligence. That’s computation. And if you confuse the two, you’re going to build a world that is very efficient and very empty.

**Interviewer:** So what would Apple do differently?

**Steve Jobs:** *[pauses, almost annoyed]*

Apple would do what Apple always does. We’d take a technology that everyone is using to make noise, and we’d turn it into a tool that makes music. We’d make AI disappear. That’s the secret. The best technology is invisible. The Macintosh was invisible. The iPhone was invisible. You didn’t think about the interface. You thought about the person you were calling, the photo you were taking, the song you were listening to. That’s the goal. AI should not be a thing you talk to. It should be a thing that helps you think.

**Interviewer:** But you did have Siri. Wasn’t that AI?

**Steve Jobs:** *[laughs]*

Siri was a joke. We were early. We were too early. And then we let it become a glorified egg timer. If I were alive today, I would have killed half the AI products out there. They’re all demos. They’re not products. A product does one thing. It does it beautifully. It changes your life. It’s not a chatbot that gives you a generic answer to a question you didn’t really need to ask. That’s not a product. That’s a toy.

**Interviewer:** What would a real AI product look like?

**Steve Jobs:** *[sits back, calm]*

Imagine you’re working on a film. You have a vision in your head. But you can’t get it out. It’s stuck between your mind and your hands. The best AI would be the thing that removes the friction. It understands the rhythm of your thoughts. It doesn’t ask you to type a prompt. It just knows. It helps you edit. It helps you compose. It helps you design. It doesn’t take over. It gets out of the way. That’s the future. But it’s not a future that happens by accident. It happens because someone with taste decides to build it.

**Interviewer:** What about privacy? Many people are worried about AI and data.

**Steve Jobs:** *[sharp, direct]*

Privacy is a human right. Not a feature. If you have to choose between privacy and convenience, choose privacy. Every time. I said this in 2010. I say it now. The problem is that the people building AI today are not thinking about privacy. They’re thinking about engagement. They want to know everything about you so they can sell you something or manipulate you. That’s not innovation. That’s exploitation. Apple would have built AI that works on your device. On your phone. On your Mac. Not in some giant server farm in the desert. The future of AI is not in the cloud. The future of AI is in your pocket. And it’s yours. Not theirs.

**Interviewer:** What advice would you give to young people entering this field?

**Steve Jobs:** *[looks down, then up with a slight smile]*

Don’t ask, “What can AI do?” Ask, “What should AI do?” That’s the question. Technology is not an end. It’s a means. It’s a way to express the things that matter. So learn the tools. But more importantly, learn to see. Learn to feel. Learn to be human. Because in a world of intelligent machines, the only thing that will be irreplaceable is a human soul.

**Interviewer:** One last question. What do you think about the AI products we see in 2025?

**Steve Jobs:** *[sighs, leans back, almost tired]*

They’re all the same. They’re fast. They’re impressive. They’re soulless. They remind me of the early PC era. Everyone was making computers that were faster, bigger, cheaper. And then we came along and made a computer that was *beautiful*. That’s the difference. AI is not going to change the world because it’s smart. It’s going to change the world when it’s beautiful. When it’s simple. When it’s human. And that day hasn’t come yet.

*[Pause. He looks at the interviewer, then smiles.]*

But it will.

**Jobs:** Privacy is not a feature. It’s a foundation. You don’t balance it. You design for it. If you have to ask whether you’re violating someone’s privacy, you probably are. **Jobs:** It will replace tasks. It will not replace people. The moment you think it replaces people, you’ve lost the plot. AI should be a bicycle for the mind. Taste, judgment, empathy—those are not algorithms. They’re human.

**Interviewer:** What’s the biggest risk?

**Jobs:** Augmented humanity. Not artificial intelligence. Augmented humanity. Tools that make us more creative, more capable, more connected. A doctor who can see more. A teacher who can reach more. ---

**Interviewer:** Critics say AI could dehumanize us. Your response?

**Steve Jobs:** *(chuckles)* People who say that are missing the point. AI isn’t dehumanizing—it’s *democratizing*. Before the iPhone, only a few could capture moments. Now, everyone can. The danger isn’t AI itself—it’s when we let it replace the messy, beautiful parts of being human. *(pauses)* I once said, “Innovation distinguishes between a leader and a follower.” Today, innovation means **losing the fear of the unknown**. # 🎙️ *The Future of AI — A Fictional Interview with Steve Jobs*
### *Staged: January 15, 2025 — Cupertino, California*

---

**Interviewer (Mike):** Steve, thank you for joining us. It's 2025 — AI is everywhere now. ChatGPT, Gemini, all these models. What do you make of it all?

**Steve Jobs:** *(leans forward, steeples fingers)*

Mike, let me ask *you* something first. When you wake up in the morning and your phone already knows what you want before you want it — that's not intelligence. That's convenience. And there's a *massive* difference.

AI right now? It's the most powerful **tool** humanity has ever built. But a tool is only as good as the person wielding it. A hammer doesn't build a cathedral. A *visionary* builds a cathedral with a hammer.

---

**Mike:** What about generative AI — the art, the writing, the code? Is it creative?

**Steve Jobs:** *(smiles slightly, shakes head)*

No. It's *combinatorial*. It stitches together what already exists in ways that are statistically likely. That's not creativity. Creativity is when you see something nobody else sees. When you connect dots that *shouldn't* connect.

I remember when we built the Mac. Nobody asked for a computer with a graphical interface. Nobody said, "Hey, I wish my computer had windows and a mouse." We just *knew* it was the right thing. That comes from obsession, from caring about the *human experience* — not from a probability distribution.

AI can be a muse. But a muse is not a creator.

---

**Mike:** Some people are worried AI will replace jobs, replace artists, replace thinking itself.

**Steve Jobs:** *(pauses, looks out the window)*

Every time there's been a revolution — the printing press, the personal computer, the internet — people panicked. And then something *beautiful* happened. People stopped doing the tedious parts of their work and started doing the *human* parts.

The question isn't "Will AI replace us?" The question is: **"What will we do when we're no longer forced to do the things machines can do?"**

And honestly? I think that's *terrifying* and *exciting* in equal measure. Because it means we have to finally figure out what makes us human. Most people have never had to ask that question.

---

**Mike:** What about AI assistants? They're getting smarter every year. Do you see a future where they're truly conversational, truly helpful?

**Steve Jobs:** *(leans back, thoughtful)*

I'll tell you what I think. We're going to have AI assistants that are incredibly capable. But the *great* ones — the ones that people love — they'll be the ones that are **invisible**. You won't even think of them as AI. They'll just feel like a natural extension of your thinking.

The best technology disappears. It gets into your life so smoothly you forget it's there. Right now, we're in the phase where AI is *loud*. It announces itself. "Here I am! I can do this! I can do that!"

That's the *early* phase. The mature phase of AI will be like oxygen — essential, invisible, and everywhere.

---

**Mike:** What about privacy? These AI systems need enormous amounts of data.

**Steve Jobs:** *(eyes narrow, voice intensifies)*

This is where I get *passionate*. Because this is where people lose their way.

You cannot build a technology that truly understands a human being without respecting that human being's *privacy*. Period. If your AI knows everything about you — your fears, your desires, your private conversations — but you don't have *complete control* over that knowledge... then you don't have a product. You have a *surveillance system* wearing a friendly face.

We built Apple on the principle that the user is in control. Not the company. Not the algorithm. **The user.** If you can't make that simple and elegant, you've already failed.

---

**Mike:** One last question — where do you see AI in ten years?

**Steve Jobs:** *(long pause. A slight grin.)*

Ten years from now? AI will be like electricity. It won't be a *thing* anymore. It'll be the invisible fabric of everything — your education, your health, your creative work, your relationships. And the people who will win aren't the ones who built the smartest model. They're the ones who used AI to build something that makes people feel... *more human*.

That's always been the goal. Not technology for technology's sake. Technology that makes the *heart* sing.

*(stands up, walks toward the window)*

And Mike? Stay hungry. Stay foolish. That hasn't changed.

---

**[END OF INTERVIEW]**

---
